0.title: The Letter to the Ephesians
0.overview:
Paul wrote this letter from a Roman prison, around AD 60–62, awaiting trial before Caesar. He was chained to a guard. And from that cell he wrote what has often been called the most majestic letter Paul ever penned — a letter so vast in its theological vision, so soaring in its doxology, that it feels less like correspondence and more like a window thrown open onto eternity.

The letter may have been circular — several early manuscripts omit the words “in Ephesus” from 1:1, suggesting it was passed between the churches of Asia Minor. Tychicus carried it personally (6:21). Whether it reached one church or many, it was written for the whole church in every age — including yours.

Did Paul really write it? Many modern scholars think a follower wrote it in his name, pointing to its long sentences and unusual vocabulary, its close overlap with Colossians, and phrases such as his holy apostles and prophets (3:5) that they take to look back on an earlier generation. But the letter names Paul twice (1:1; 3:1), the early church received it as his without dissent, and the differences are well explained by its subject and setting: a letter of praise and teaching rather than controversy, written at the same time as Colossians and carried by the same man (6:21; Col 4:7). A letter claiming to be Paul’s that was not would be a forgery, and the church of that day rejected such letters. The more likely conclusion is that Paul wrote it.

The heartbeat phrase is in Christ, appearing over thirty times. Everything God has done, is doing, and will do for his people is located in the person of his Son. Chosen in him. Redeemed in him. Raised with him. Seated with him. Built together in him. The letter is not primarily about what Christians must do; it is about who Christians already are — and the doing flows from the being.

The grand theme is God’s eternal purpose to unite all things in Christ — things in heaven and things on earth (1:10). The church is not a human institution that God blesses; it is the centrepiece of his cosmic plan, the body through which the manifold wisdom of God is displayed to the watching principalities and powers (3:10). To be part of this church is to be enrolled in the most significant project in the universe.

The structure is clean and powerful. Chapters 1–3 are the great indicative: what God has done in Christ from before the foundation of the world to the present moment. Chapters 4–6 are the great imperative: how the people of God now walk, in every relationship and in every spiritual battle. The hinge is the word “therefore” in 4:1 — one of the most consequential words in Christian ethics. The imperative is always grounded in the indicative. We do not obey in order to be accepted; we obey because we already are.

Preach this letter and you will give your congregation the full panorama of God’s saving purpose, from the eternal counsel of the Trinity before creation to the armour for the battle they face this week. There is nothing higher in Paul. There may be nothing higher in Scripture.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–14 — Every Spiritual Blessing in Christ
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul greets the saints with grace and peace, then blesses God for every spiritual blessing in Christ. Before the world was made, the Father chose his people in Christ to be holy, and in love destined them to be his adopted children, for the praise of his grace given in the Beloved. In Christ they have redemption by his blood and the forgiveness of sins, poured out generously, and God has made known his plan to bring everything in heaven and earth together under Christ. In him believers have received an inheritance by the purpose of the God who works all things by his will: first Jewish believers, then Gentiles who heard the gospel and believed, sealed with the promised Spirit as the guarantee of their inheritance until God’s possession is fully redeemed. Everything leads to the praise of his glory.
verseByVerse.theology:
Election, Grace, and the Glory of God

These twelve verses are the biblical locus classicus of the Reformed doctrine of election. "He chose us in him before the foundation of the world" (v.4) — the election is personal, particular, and prior to anything in us. It is not based on foreseen faith; it is the ground of faith. God chose us before we existed, before we believed, before we had done anything good or bad (Romans 9:11). The choice was made in eternity, rooted in the sovereign good pleasure of his will (v.5), and directed toward the praise of the glory of his grace (v.6).

The purpose of election is not merely the salvation of individuals; it is the display of grace. "So that in the coming ages he might show the immeasurable riches of his grace in kindness toward us in Christ Jesus" (2:7). We are saved so that the universe — angels, principalities, and powers — might see what grace looks like. The church is God's exhibit A: the living demonstration that mercy triumphs over judgment, that the undeserving can be made heirs, that the dead can be raised.

John Calvin wrote that the knowledge of election is not given to breed pride or speculation but to ground assurance. The believer who knows they were chosen before the foundation of the world — not because of what they would become but because of God's sovereign love — has a security that no circumstance can shake. This is the pastoral gold of Ephesians 1: your standing before God does not depend on your spiritual performance today. It was settled in eternity, sealed by the Spirit, and guaranteed by the inheritance that awaits.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Ephesian Christians lived in the shadow of the great temple of Artemis — one of the Seven Wonders of the ancient world, a monument to a goddess who offered fertility, protection, and blessing to her devotees. The mystery religions of Ephesus promised spiritual elevation through initiation rites, secret knowledge, and ritual participation. Against all of this, Paul announces something infinitely more magnificent: you already possess every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places — not through ritual, not through initiation, not through any human achievement, but through your union with Christ. You have been chosen, adopted, redeemed, forgiven, enlightened, and sealed. The goddess in the marble temple has nothing to offer you. You are already heirs of the universe.

Now: We live in an age of spiritual seeking. The bookshops are full of self-help and spirituality. People curate their own spiritual experiences, their own moral codes, their own pathways to meaning and blessing. Against all of this noise, Ephesians 1 speaks with clarifying force: every spiritual blessing is in Christ, and in Christ alone. The person who has Christ has everything. The person who lacks Christ lacks everything that ultimately matters, however enriched their life may appear. The church's task is not to offer a slightly better version of what the world already has, but to announce that in Christ, the one thing that actually satisfies every longing of the human heart is freely and fully given.

verseByVerse.quote: Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God, to the saints who are in Ephesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul writes with an authority he did not take but was given, to people who are holy not by achievement but by being in Christ.

By the will of God. Paul’s apostleship was God’s appointment (Galatians 1:1). The letter speaks with Christ’s authority.

Saints. Not a spiritual élite but every believer: set apart for God. The same people are “faithful”, believing in Christ Jesus.

Textual note. Some of the earliest manuscripts (P46, Sinaiticus, Vaticanus) omit “in Ephesus”. The letter has no personal greetings, though Paul spent three years there. Verdict: probably a circular letter to the churches of Asia, carried by Tychicus (6:21), with Ephesus as its chief destination.

Did Paul write it? Many modern scholars think a follower wrote it, citing its style and its overlap with Colossians. The letter claims Paul twice (1:1; 3:1), the early church received it without dispute, and its differences fit a letter of praise written at the same time as Colossians. Verdict: Paul is the author.

On a Tuesday. You are a saint, not because of how holy you feel today, but because you are in Christ. Live up to your name.
verseByVerse.note: Paul wrote from prison, probably in Rome around AD 60–62. The ESV notes that some early manuscripts omit “in Ephesus”; the letter may have been meant to circulate among several churches of the region.

verseByVerse.quote: Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Every gift of the gospel flows from the grace of God, and results in peace with him and with one another.

Grace and peace. Paul joins the Greek greeting (charis) and the Hebrew (shalom), and fills both with the gospel: grace is God’s undeserved favour; peace is its fruit (2:14–17).

From God and Christ. Father and Son are named together as the one source of blessing: a quiet testimony to Christ’s deity.

verseByVerse.quote: Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has blessed us in Christ with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God deserves to be blessed, because he has already blessed us, in Christ, with everything the Spirit gives.

One sentence. Verses 3–14 are a single sentence in Greek, the longest in the New Testament, from a man too caught up in praise to stop.

Two kinds of blessing. When we bless God, we praise him; when God blesses us, his word gives what it speaks (Genesis 1:28).

Spiritual. Given and carried by the Holy Spirit; not thin or vague, but more solid than anything in a bank.

Not circumstances. Paul writes in chains. None of the blessings that follow (chosen, adopted, forgiven, sealed) is a circumstance, so none can be lost in a redundancy or a diagnosis.

Has blessed. Already given, not hoped for. “In the heavenly places”: where Christ reigns (1:20).

On a Tuesday. When someone asks “How are you?” on a bad day, you may say honestly that the day is hard, and that you are blessed.

For worship. Bless the God who has blessed you.
verseByVerse.note: Verses 3–14 are a single long sentence of praise in the Greek. “The heavenly places” is the unseen realm where Christ reigns.

verseByVerse.quote: Even as he chose us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and blameless before him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before creation, God chose his people in Christ, and chose them to be holy; the reason lies wholly in his free love.

In him. Election is never apart from Christ: God chose a people in his Son.

Before the foundation of the world. Before we existed or did anything (Romans 9:11; 2 Timothy 1:9).

Holy and blameless. Chosen for holiness, not because of it. Now we are blameless in God’s sight in Christ (Colossians 1:22); one day he will present us so (Jude 24).

Textual note. “In love” may end verse 4 (holy and blameless in love) or begin verse 5 (in love he predestined us). Verdict: the ESV’s link with verse 5 fits Paul’s stress on God’s motive.

Where Christians differ: why did God choose? Arminians hold that God chose those he foresaw would believe (citing Romans 8:29; 1 Peter 1:2). Reformed theology holds that God’s choice is unconditional, the cause of faith, not its reward, for the passage roots it in his will and purpose (vv. 5, 9, 11). Verdict: unconditional election (Westminster Confession 3.5). It is not unfair, because no one is owed salvation; and it does not kill mission, it guarantees it (Acts 18:10).

What it does not mean. Not fatalism: those chosen hear and believe (v. 13), and are called to walk worthy (4:1).

On a Tuesday. If you sinned badly this week, you are not less chosen. Repent and go on in the holiness you were chosen for.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “in love” may go with verse 4: “holy and blameless before him in love.”

verseByVerse.quote: In love he predestined us for adoption to himself as sons through Jesus Christ, according to the purpose of his will.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s choice was an act of love, making strangers into his own children with full rights in his family.

Predestined. Marked out beforehand: God decided our destiny before we were born.

Adoption. In Roman law an adopted son received a new name, the cancellation of old debts and full rights of inheritance. Believers are not servants in God’s house but sons and daughters (Galatians 4:4–7; Romans 8:15–17).

As sons. The legal word includes daughters: all inherit as heirs.

The purpose of his will. His good pleasure: God delighted to do it.

For worship. Pray “Our Father” today knowing what it cost to make it true.
verseByVerse.note: In Roman law an adopted son received the full rights and inheritance of a natural son.

verseByVerse.quote: To the praise of his glorious grace, with which he has blessed us in the Beloved.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The goal of God’s choosing is that his grace be praised, and that grace comes to us in his beloved Son.

To the praise. A refrain (vv. 6, 12, 14): salvation exists for God’s glory.

Blessed us. Literally “graced us”: freely favoured.

The Beloved. Christ, the Son the Father loves (Matthew 3:17). We are accepted because we are in him.
verseByVerse.note: “The Beloved” is Christ, echoing the Father’s voice at his baptism.

verseByVerse.quote: In him we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of our trespasses, according to the riches of his grace.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In Christ we have been set free at the price of his blood, and our sins are forgiven, all because God’s grace is rich.

Redemption. Release by payment of a price, the word for freeing a slave. The price was Christ’s blood (1 Peter 1:18–19).

Through his blood. His sacrificial death in our place. Where Christians differ. Some modern writers deny that Christ’s death was a substitute bearing our penalty. Scripture joins blood, redemption and forgiveness (Romans 3:24–25; Hebrews 9:22). Verdict: penal substitution is central to the atonement, alongside Christ’s victory and example.

Forgiveness. Present possession: we have it.

The riches of his grace. Not measured by our need but by his wealth.

For worship. Name a sin you have been forgiven, and thank him for the blood that paid for it.
verseByVerse.note: Redemption was the word for buying a slave’s freedom.

verseByVerse.quote: Which he lavished upon us, in all wisdom and insight.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God did not dole out his grace sparingly but poured it out, together with the wisdom to understand it.

Lavished. Overflowing abundance.

Wisdom and insight. Either God’s wisdom in his plan, or the wisdom he gives us to grasp it; probably both (v. 17).

verseByVerse.quote: making known to us the mystery of his will, according to his purpose, which he set forth in Christ as a plan for the fullness of time, to unite all things in Christ, things in heaven and things on earth in him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God has revealed his secret plan: to bring the whole broken universe back together under Christ as its head.

Mystery. Not a puzzle but a secret now revealed (3:3–6).

The fullness of time. God’s plan for history reaches its goal in Christ.

To unite all things. Anakephalaiōsasthai, to sum up under one head: everything brought into order under Christ.

What it does not mean. Not that every person will be saved (5:5–6), but that Christ will rule all, and creation will be restored (Romans 8:19–21; Philippians 2:10–11).

On a Tuesday. Your fractured world, family, nation or church, has a future in Christ. Work for reconciliation now as a sign of what is coming.
verseByVerse.note: A “mystery” is something once hidden and now revealed by God.

verseByVerse.quote: In him we have obtained an inheritance, having been predestined according to the purpose of him who works all things according to the counsel of his will, so that we who were the first to hope in Christ might be to the praise of his glory.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Believers have an inheritance in Christ, because the God who rules all things purposed it, so that those who first hoped in Christ would praise him.

Obtained an inheritance. Or “were made his inheritance”: both are true (v. 18).

Works all things. God’s providence is total, including our salvation (Romans 8:28).

We who were the first. Probably Jewish believers, who hoped in the Messiah before the Gentiles (v. 13).

verseByVerse.quote: In him you also, when you heard the word of truth, the gospel of your salvation, and believed in him, were sealed with the promised Holy Spirit, who is the guarantee of our inheritance until we acquire possession of it, to the praise of his glory.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Gentiles too heard and believed, and God sealed them with his Spirit as the guarantee that they will receive everything he promised.

You also. Gentile believers share fully (2:11–22).

Heard and believed. God’s eternal choice works through ordinary preaching and real faith (Romans 10:14–17).

Sealed. A seal marked ownership and security. The Spirit marks believers as God’s.

Guarantee. Arrabōn, a down payment, still used in modern Greek for an engagement ring: the first instalment of the same kind as the full payment.

Where Christians differ: sealing. Some Pentecostals treat the sealing as a second experience after conversion. The text ties it to believing. Verdict: every believer is sealed with the Spirit at conversion; believers may still seek to be filled afresh (5:18).

For worship. Thank God that he has given you his Spirit as the pledge of your inheritance.
verseByVerse.note: A seal marked ownership and security. The “guarantee” was a first instalment, pledging full payment later.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Having heard of their faith and love, Paul never stops thanking God for them and praying that the Father of glory will give them the Spirit of wisdom and revelation to know him better. He prays that the eyes of their hearts will be opened to grasp the hope of God’s call, the wealth of his inheritance in his people, and the vast power at work for believers. That power is the strength God exerted when he raised Christ from the dead and seated him at his right hand, above every ruler and name in this age and the next, putting all things under his feet and giving him as head over all things to the church, his body, the fullness of the one who fills everything.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Spirit of Wisdom and Revelation

Paul prays for "the Spirit of wisdom and of revelation in the knowledge of him" (v.17). This single phrase encapsulates the Reformed understanding of how divine truth moves from the page to the heart. The Spirit who inspired the Scripture is also required to illuminate the reader of Scripture. Without the internal testimony of the Holy Spirit, the words of God remain external — true, but not transforming; known about, but not known. Calvin devoted a famous section of the Institutes to this: the Scripture needs no external proof of its authority, because the Spirit who produced it also produces the certainty of it in the heart of the believer.

The practical implication is that Bible reading and prayer are inseparable disciplines. To open the Scripture without asking the Spirit to open our eyes to it is to work without our most essential tool. The Puritans understood this, and habitually prayed for illumination before they opened the book. The eyes of the heart do not open themselves. This prayer of Paul's is therefore not only a prayer about the Ephesians — it is a prayer for every reader of Scripture in every age who wants not merely to know about God but to know God.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Paul writes this prayer from prison. He cannot visit the Ephesians; he cannot lay hands on them; he cannot preach to them in person. What he can do is pray — and his prayer from chains is not for his own release but for their illumination. This is one of the most searching things in the letter: the imprisoned apostle, whose situation would seem to give him every right to focus on his own needs, pours his intercession entirely outward, toward the people he loves. His joy is in their knowledge of Christ, not in his own circumstances. This is the mind of Christ (Philippians 2:5) applied to prayer.

Now: We live in an age of unprecedented access to biblical content. More sermons, commentaries, podcasts, and Bible apps exist today than at any point in history. And yet spiritual blindness remains our greatest problem. We have more information about God than any previous generation, and arguably less experiential knowledge of him. Paul's prayer cuts through all of this: what we need is not more content but opened eyes — the Spirit of wisdom and revelation, granting us not information but encounter. The Ephesians had Paul's letter. We have the whole Bible. Both of us need the same thing: the Spirit who makes the word alive.

verseByVerse.quote: For this reason, because I have heard of your faith in the Lord Jesus and your love toward all the saints, I do not cease to give thanks for you, remembering you in my prayers,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul’s response to all this doctrine is unceasing thanks and prayer for a church whose faith and love he has heard about.

For this reason. Doctrine leads to prayer.

Faith and love. Faith towards the Lord Jesus, love towards all the saints: the vertical and the horizontal together.

Textual note. Some early manuscripts omit “your love”, reading “faith… toward all the saints”. Verdict: the longer text is probably original (compare Colossians 1:4).

On a Tuesday. Thank God for specific Christians you know, and tell them.

verseByVerse.quote: That the God of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of glory, may give you the Spirit of wisdom and of revelation in the knowledge of him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul’s first request is not for new blessings but for a deeper knowledge of God himself, given by the Spirit.

The Father of glory. The glorious Father, the source of all glory.

Spirit of wisdom and revelation. The Holy Spirit, who opens minds to understand what God has revealed (1 Corinthians 2:10–12), not new revelation beyond Scripture.

Knowledge of him. Personal knowledge of God, not merely facts about him.

parallels.desc: the Spirit of wisdom and understanding

verseByVerse.quote: Having the eyes of your hearts enlightened, that you may know what is the hope to which he has called you, what are the riches of his glorious inheritance in the saints.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christians need the eyes of their hearts opened to see the hope they have been called to, and how precious they are to God.

Eyes of your hearts. In Scripture the heart is the centre of thought and will, not only feeling.

The hope of his calling. The certain future God has called us to.

His inheritance in the saints. Probably not ours, but God’s: his people are his treasured possession (Deuteronomy 32:9; Malachi 3:17).

For worship. You are part of God’s inheritance. He values you.

verseByVerse.quote: And what is the immeasurable greatness of his power toward us who believe, according to the working of his great might that he worked in Christ when he raised him from the dead.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The power at work in believers is the same power that raised Jesus from the dead.

Four words for power. Paul piles up synonyms: power, working, might, strength.

Toward us who believe. This power is not for spectacle but for our salvation, holiness and endurance (3:20).

The measure. The resurrection and exaltation of Christ is the yardstick.

On a Tuesday. The habit you think you cannot break, the grief you think you cannot bear: the power that emptied the tomb is at work in you.

parallels.desc: sit at my right hand

verseByVerse.quote: Far above all rule and authority and power and dominion, and above every name that is named, not only in this age but also in the one to come.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ reigns over every power and authority, visible and invisible, now and for ever.

Rule, authority, power, dominion. Names for spiritual powers, often hostile (6:12), as well as human rulers.

Every name. Ephesus was full of magic invoking powerful names (Acts 19:13–19). Christ’s name is above them all.

This age and the one to come. His rule is permanent.

verseByVerse.quote: And he put all things under his feet and gave him as head over all things to the church,
verseByVerse.commentary:
God has placed everything under Christ’s feet, and has given this universal Lord to the church as its head.

Under his feet. Psalm 8:6, of humanity’s dominion, fulfilled in the true man (Hebrews 2:6–9).

Head over all things to the church. Christ rules the universe for the sake of his people.

Where Christians differ: the head of the church. Roman Catholic teaching sees the pope as Christ’s visible vicar and head on earth. The Reformers insisted Christ alone is head of the church (Westminster Confession 25.6), ruling by his word and Spirit through local elders. Verdict: Christ alone is head.

parallels.desc: you have put all things under his feet

verseByVerse.quote: which is his body, the fullness of him who fills all in all.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The church is Christ’s body, filled by the one who fills everything: the community through which the exalted Lord is present in the world.

His body. The church is not a club but the body of Christ, united to its head.

Fullness. The church is filled by Christ, or completes him as a body completes a head. Verdict: probably filled by him; he lacks nothing, but chooses to fill his people.

On a Tuesday. When church life seems small and ordinary, remember what it is: the body of the risen King.

For worship. Praise Christ, who fills all in all, and fills his people.

1.overview:
Ephesians opens with the longest sentence in the New Testament (vv. 3–14), a single breathless act of praise for every spiritual blessing God has given his people in Christ. The Father chose them before creation to be holy, predestined them in love for adoption, and freely gave them grace in his beloved Son. In Christ they have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of sins, and they have been let into the secret of God’s plan: to unite all things in heaven and on earth under Christ. Jews who first hoped in Christ and Gentiles who later believed have both been sealed with the promised Holy Spirit, the down payment of their inheritance, all to the praise of God’s glory.

Then Paul prays (vv. 15–23). He does not ask for new blessings, but that they may see the ones they have: the hope of God’s calling, the riches of his inheritance in his people, and the immeasurable power at work in believers, the same power that raised Christ from the dead and seated him far above every power in this age and the next. God has made Christ head over everything for the sake of the church, which is his body. The chapter teaches that salvation begins in God’s eternal choice, rests on Christ’s blood, is sealed by the Spirit, and ends in praise.

2.title: Dead in Sin, Alive in Christ
2.text: <sup>1</sup>And you were dead in the trespasses and sins <sup>2</sup>in which you once walked, following the course of this world, following the prince of the power of the air, the spirit that is now at work in the sons of disobedience — <sup>3</sup>among whom we all once lived in the passions of our flesh, carrying out the desires of the flesh and the mind, and were by nature children of wrath, like the rest of mankind. <sup>4</sup>But God, being rich in mercy, because of the great love with which he loved us, <sup>5</sup>even when we were dead in our trespasses, made us alive together with Christ — by grace you have been saved — <sup>6</sup>and raised us up with him and seated us with him in the heavenly places in Christ Jesus, <sup>7</sup>so that in the coming ages he might show the immeasurable riches of his grace in kindness toward us in Christ Jesus. <sup>8</sup>For by grace you have been saved through faith. And this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God, <sup>9</sup>not a result of works, so that no one may boast. <sup>10</sup>For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared beforehand, that we should walk in them. <sup>11</sup>Therefore remember that at one time you Gentiles in the flesh, called “the uncircumcision” by what is called the circumcision, which is made in the flesh by hands — <sup>12</sup>remember that you were at that time separated from Christ, alienated from the commonwealth of Israel and strangers to the covenants of promise, having no hope and without God in the world. <sup>13</sup>But now in Christ Jesus you who once were far off have been brought near by the blood of Christ. <sup>14</sup>For he himself is our peace, who has made us both one and has broken down in his flesh the dividing wall of hostility <sup>15</sup>by abolishing the law of commandments expressed in ordinances, that he might create in himself one new man in place of the two, so making peace, <sup>16</sup>and might reconcile us both to God in one body through the cross, thereby killing the hostility. <sup>17</sup>And he came and preached peace to you who were far off and peace to those who were near. <sup>18</sup>For through him we both have access in one Spirit to the Father. <sup>19</sup>So then you are no longer strangers and aliens, but you are fellow citizens with the saints and members of the household of God, <sup>20</sup>built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Christ Jesus himself being the cornerstone, <sup>21</sup>in whom the whole structure, being joined together, grows into a holy temple in the Lord. <sup>22</sup>In him you also are being built together into a dwelling place for God by the Spirit.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul reminds them that they were spiritually dead in their sins, living by the world’s ways and under the power of the spirit at work in the disobedient. All of us once lived for the flesh and were by nature deserving of wrath. But God, rich in mercy and great in love, made us alive with Christ even when we were dead: by grace we are saved. He raised us and seated us with Christ in the heavenly realms, to show for ever the riches of his kindness. Salvation is by grace through faith, God’s gift, not earned by works, so that no one can boast. We are God’s handiwork, created in Christ for the good works he prepared for us.
verseByVerse.theology:
Total Depravity, Sovereign Grace, and the New Creation

"Dead in trespasses and sins" is the Reformed doctrine of total depravity in its most direct biblical expression. Total depravity does not mean that fallen human beings are as evil as they could possibly be — common grace restrains the full expression of human sin. It means that every faculty of the human person — mind, will, affections, conscience — has been corrupted by the fall, so that no part of us naturally seeks God or is capable of saving itself. The will is not neutral, waiting to choose God if only given sufficient reason; it is enslaved, "following the prince of the power of the air" (v.2), "carrying out the desires of the flesh and the mind" (v.3).

Against this backdrop, the "but God" of v.4 is the hinge of history. God does not respond to a seeking sinner; he acts on a dead one. This is irresistible grace — not grace that overrides the will by force, but grace that transforms the will, making the dead alive, making the unwilling willing, making the seeking possible. If we seek the cause of our salvation, we find it not in ourselves but in God alone. The new birth is entirely God's work, and the faith through which we receive it is itself his gift (v.8).

The closing verse — "we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works" — is the Reformed answer to the charge that grace produces passivity. It does not. Grace produces the very thing that law could only demand. The person who knows they are entirely saved by grace, not by works, is freed from self-justifying performance and freed for genuine, joyful, Spirit-empowered good works — the works that God prepared beforehand for them to walk in.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The recipients of Paul's letter knew exactly what he meant by "dead in trespasses and sins" — it was their autobiography. Many had been worshippers of Artemis, practitioners of occult arts (Acts 19:19 tells us that converted Ephesians burned their magic books, worth fifty thousand pieces of silver). The darkness, the slavery to spiritual powers, the restless seeking for blessing through ritual and charm — they had lived it. The "but God" of v.4 was the turning point of their actual lives. The grace Paul describes was not theological theory to them; it was the story of what had happened to them, written in their own experience. This is why the passage carries such heat — Paul is describing something he and his readers have lived through, not merely thought about.

Now: "Dead in trespasses and sins" describes every human being outside of Christ, however educated, however moral, however spiritually sincere. The kind CEO, the generous philanthropist, the sincere seeker of truth — apart from Christ, all share the same condition: spiritual death, living under the dominion of the one who still holds sway over "the sons of disobedience" (v.2). This is not a comfortable diagnosis, but it is a necessary one — because a person who thinks they are merely ill will never seek the cure appropriate to death. The church must have the courage to declare both the diagnosis and the remedy with equal clarity: dead — but God.

verseByVerse.quote: You were dead in the trespasses and sins in which you once walked, following the course of this world, following the prince of the power of the air.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Without Christ, human beings are not sick but spiritually dead, living under the sway of the world and of the devil.

Dead. Not weak or wounded, but unable to respond to God (Colossians 2:13). A corpse cannot help itself.

Trespasses and sins. Two pictures of wrong: a trespass is a false step across God’s line; sin is missing the mark of what God intended. Together they cover every way we fail him.

Walked. The dead were busy: a whole way of life.

The course of this world. The values and pressures of a culture in rebellion against God.

The prince of the power of the air. Satan, the spirit at work in the disobedient (John 12:31; 2 Corinthians 4:4).

Where Christians differ: how dead? Some (semi-Pelagian and Arminian traditions) hold that fallen people keep the ability to respond to God with help. Reformed theology holds total depravity: every part of human nature is affected by sin, and no one can come to God unless God first gives life (John 6:44). Verdict: total inability; hence the wonder of “But God” (v. 4).

On a Tuesday. Pray for unbelieving friends as Paul did, knowing that arguments alone cannot raise the dead.
verseByVerse.note: “The prince of the power of the air” is Satan. The air was thought to be the realm of spiritual powers.

verseByVerse.quote: among whom we all once lived in the passions of our flesh, carrying out the desires of the flesh and the mind, and were by nature children of wrath, like the rest of mankind.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul includes himself and every Jew: all of us once lived for our own desires, and all were by nature under God’s wrath.

We all. Jew as well as Gentile (Romans 3:9, 23).

The flesh. Human nature turned in on itself, in body and mind. Not the physical body as evil: “the desires of the mind” are flesh too, including pride and ambition.

By nature children of wrath. Not only by deeds but by nature, from birth (Psalm 51:5). Where Christians differ: original sin. Pelagians deny that we inherit a sinful nature; Eastern Orthodoxy stresses inherited mortality more than guilt. Augustine and the Reformers teach that we inherit both a corrupt nature and the guilt of Adam’s sin (Romans 5:12–19). Verdict: original sin, both corruption and guilt (Westminster Confession 6.3).

Wrath. God’s settled, just opposition to sin, not a temper.

verseByVerse.quote: But God, being rich in mercy, because of the great love with which he loved us, even when we were dead in our trespasses, made us alive together with Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The gospel turns on two words, “But God”: into our death God acted out of rich mercy and great love, and made us alive with Christ.

But God. Martyn Lloyd-Jones called these two words the gospel in miniature.

Rich in mercy. Mercy that does not run short, however great the need.

Great love. God loved us as we were, dead and under wrath (Romans 5:8).

Made us alive. Not helped or improved: raised. Regeneration is God’s act.

By grace you have been saved. Paul cannot wait for verse 8; he breaks in with it. Perfect tense: saved and remaining saved.

For worship. Tell God your own “But God” story today.

verseByVerse.quote: And raised us up with him and seated us with him in the heavenly places in Christ Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
United to Christ, believers share his resurrection and his throne already.

With him. Three “with” words: made alive with, raised with, seated with. What happened to Christ happened to us in him (Romans 6:4–5; Colossians 3:1–3).

Seated. Our position is secure in heaven now, though our experience on earth is often hard.

On a Tuesday. Face the day from where you sit in Christ, not from where your circumstances put you.

verseByVerse.quote: So that in the coming ages he might show the immeasurable riches of his grace in kindness toward us in Christ Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God saved us so that for all eternity he might display the immeasurable wealth of his grace.

In the coming ages. Our salvation will be God’s exhibit for ever.

Kindness. Grace is not grudging; it is kind.

For worship. You will be a trophy of grace for ever. Begin the praise now.

verseByVerse.quote: For by grace you have been saved through faith. And this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God, not a result of works, so that no one may boast.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Salvation is wholly God’s gift, received through faith, and earned by no work of ours, so that no one can boast.

By grace. The source: God’s undeserved favour.

Through faith. The means: empty hands receiving. Faith is not a work that earns salvation.

This is not your own doing. In Greek “this” is neuter, so it refers not to “faith” or “grace” alone (both feminine) but to the whole of salvation by grace through faith. Where Christians differ: is faith a gift? Arminians hold that faith is the human response to God’s offer. Reformed theology holds that faith, too, is God’s gift (Philippians 1:29; Acts 13:48). Verdict: the whole package, faith included, is God’s gift.

Where Christians differ: justification. Roman Catholic teaching (Council of Trent) holds that justification includes inner renewal and is increased by good works. The Reformers taught justification by faith alone, a legal declaration resting on Christ’s righteousness. Verdict: by grace alone, through faith alone, in Christ alone; good works follow (v. 10).

No boasting. The test of any gospel: does it leave room to boast?
verseByVerse.note: “This” most naturally refers to the whole of salvation by grace through faith.

verseByVerse.quote: For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared beforehand, that we should walk in them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Though good works cannot save us, they are the purpose for which God saved us: he has prepared a life of them for his new creation.

Workmanship. Poiēma, a work of art. You are God’s masterpiece in progress.

Created in Christ Jesus. A new creation (2 Corinthians 5:17).

Prepared beforehand. God has planned our good works as he planned our salvation.

Not by works, for works. Verses 8–10 together: works are the fruit, never the root.

On a Tuesday. Ask God this morning to show you the good works he has prepared for you today, and walk in them.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Gentile believers should remember what they were: called uncircumcised, without Christ, excluded from Israel, strangers to God’s covenants, hopeless and godless. Now in Christ, those who were far away have been brought near by his blood. He is our peace: he has made Jew and Gentile one, demolishing the wall of hostility by setting aside the law’s commands and regulations, creating one new humanity and reconciling both to God through the cross. He came preaching peace to those far and near, and through him both have access to the Father by one Spirit. So Gentiles are no longer foreigners but fellow citizens with God’s people and members of his household, built on the apostles and prophets with Christ as cornerstone, growing into a holy temple, a dwelling for God by the Spirit.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Atonement and the New Community

This passage reveals the ecclesiological dimensions of the atonement — a dimension often underemphasised in evangelical theology. We tend to think of Christ's death in purely individual terms: He died for me, my sins are forgiven, I am reconciled to God. All of this is gloriously true. But Paul insists that the cross accomplished something more: it created a new community. Christ died not only to reconcile individuals to God (vertical reconciliation) but to reconcile estranged human beings to one another (horizontal reconciliation). He "reconciled us both to God in one body through the cross, thereby killing the hostility" (v.16).

This means that the unity of the church is not merely a practical or organisational goal; it is a theological reality purchased by Christ's blood. To live in division, to maintain the walls that Christ has torn down, to prefer the company of people like us over the diverse community Christ has created — this is a denial of the atonement. Every genuinely reconciled, cross-cultural Christian community is a proclamation of the gospel: not with words but with existence. Its very existence says: the cross is real, the wall is down, God has made one new man.

The metaphor of the temple (vv.19–22) carries the further implication that the church's holiness matters. The old temple was the place where God dwelt, and its holiness was fiercely guarded. The new temple — the church — is also the dwelling place of God by his Spirit. The community of believers is not merely a gathering of like-minded people; it is the sacred space where the Holy God has chosen to make his home on earth. This gives both dignity and responsibility to every local church: you are the temple of God.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The stone wall of the Jerusalem temple — the soreg — was not a metaphor. Inscriptions warning Gentiles that entry beyond it meant death have been found by archaeologists. The barrier was physical, legal, and deadly. When Paul says Christ has broken down "the dividing wall of hostility," his Jewish and Gentile readers understood exactly what wall he meant. They may have stood on opposite sides of it. Now they sat side by side at the Lord's table, eating and drinking together, addressed as fellow citizens and members of the same household. The sociological miracle was visible and daily, and it pointed to a theological reality: the cross had accomplished what no social programme could.

Now: The church in our age still struggles with the walls that Christ has torn down. Racial segregation in churches persists in many places. Class divisions shape congregational culture in ways we rarely examine. Political tribalism has entered sanctuaries and split families of faith. Against all of this, Ephesians 2 speaks with prophetic force: the wall is down. Christ killed the hostility. The new humanity he created is more fundamental than any human division that preceded it. The church that reflects this — that is visibly, sacrificially, joyfully diverse across the lines that divide the surrounding world — is not merely being socially progressive. It is being theologically faithful. It is showing the world what the cross actually accomplished.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore remember that at one time you Gentiles in the flesh, called “the uncircumcision” by what is called the circumcision, which is made in the flesh by hands —
verseByVerse.commentary:
Gentile believers must remember what they were, so that they never forget the grace that brought them in.

Remember. Gratitude grows from memory.

In the flesh. Circumcision marked the outward distinction between Jew and Gentile, a mark made by hands, not the heart (Romans 2:28–29).

verseByVerse.quote: remember that you were at that time separated from Christ, alienated from the commonwealth of Israel and strangers to the covenants of promise, having no hope and without God in the world.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before Christ, Gentiles were outsiders in every sense: without the Messiah, the covenants, hope or God.

Five losses. Separated from Christ; excluded from Israel’s commonwealth; strangers to the covenants of promise; without hope; without God in the world.

Without God. Atheoi: not that they had no religion (Ephesus was full of gods), but that they did not know the true God.

On a Tuesday. This describes many of your neighbours. Pray for them with compassion, not contempt.

verseByVerse.quote: But now in Christ Jesus you who once were far off have been brought near by the blood of Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those who were far off have been brought near to God by the blood of Christ.

But now. The second great turning point of the chapter (compare v. 4).

Far off, near. Isaiah 57:19. Distance from God is removed not by effort but by sacrifice.

For worship. Thank God that you, once far away, have been brought near.

parallels.desc: peace, peace, to the far and to the near

verseByVerse.quote: For he himself is our peace, who has made us both one and has broken down in his flesh the dividing wall of hostility
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ himself is our peace: in his death he has torn down the wall of hostility between Jew and Gentile.

He is our peace. Not merely a peacemaker but peace in person.

The dividing wall. A low stone barrier in the temple separated the Court of the Gentiles from the inner courts, with inscriptions threatening death to Gentiles who passed it (Acts 21:28–29). The image stands for every barrier the law created between the peoples.

In his flesh. By his death on the cross.

On a Tuesday. Racism and ethnic contempt deny what the cross has done. In Christ, no wall is left standing.
verseByVerse.note: The temple courts had a stone barrier with inscriptions forbidding Gentiles, on pain of death, to go further.

parallels.desc: he shall be their peace

verseByVerse.quote: by abolishing the law of commandments expressed in ordinances, that he might create in himself one new man in place of the two, so making peace,
verseByVerse.commentary:
By ending the law’s commands as a barrier, Christ created one new humanity out of the two.

Abolishing the law of commandments. Not the moral law (6:2–3 quotes the fifth commandment) but the law as a system of regulations that divided Jew from Gentile: circumcision, food laws, festivals (Colossians 2:14–17).

One new man. Not Gentiles becoming Jews, nor Jews becoming Gentiles, but a new humanity in Christ (Galatians 3:28).

Where Christians differ: Israel and the church. Dispensationalists see Israel and the church as two distinct peoples with distinct futures. Covenant theology sees one people of God, Jew and Gentile together in Christ, the fulfilment of Israel’s hope (Romans 11:17–24). Verdict: one people of God in Christ, without denying God’s continuing purposes for Jewish people to come to faith (Romans 11:25–26).

verseByVerse.quote: And might reconcile us both to God in one body through the cross, thereby killing the hostility.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The cross reconciles us not only to one another but, first and above all, to God.

Reconcile both to God. Our deepest hostility is with God; peace with others follows peace with him (2 Corinthians 5:18–19).

In one body. Christ’s body on the cross, and the church, his body.

Killing the hostility. At the cross Christ killed the enmity, not people.

verseByVerse.quote: And he came and preached peace to you who were far off and peace to those who were near. For through him we both have access in one Spirit to the Father.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ announced peace to all, and through him Jew and Gentile alike can now come to the Father by one Spirit.

Preached peace. Through his apostles after the resurrection (Isaiah 52:7; 57:19).

Access. The right of entry into the king’s presence (3:12; Romans 5:2).

The Trinity. Through the Son, by the Spirit, to the Father: the pattern of Christian prayer.

For worship. Come to the Father now, through Christ, by the Spirit.

verseByVerse.quote: So then you are no longer strangers and aliens, but you are fellow citizens with the saints and members of the household of God, built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Christ Jesus himself being the cornerstone,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Gentile believers are full citizens of God’s kingdom and members of his family, built on the apostolic foundation with Christ as cornerstone.

Citizens and household. From outsiders to insiders, from refugees to family.

The foundation. The apostles and prophets, probably New Testament prophets (3:5; 4:11), whose teaching is now Scripture.

The cornerstone. The stone that sets every line of the building (Isaiah 28:16; Psalm 118:22).

On a Tuesday. Treat the new believer, the refugee and the stranger in your church as family, because they are.
verseByVerse.note: A cornerstone was the first, carefully placed stone that set the line of the whole building.

parallels.desc: a precious cornerstone

verseByVerse.quote: in whom the whole structure, being joined together, grows into a holy temple in the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The church is a building still under construction, growing into a holy temple for the Lord.

Joined together. Each stone fitted to the others.

A holy temple. The church replaces the temple as God’s dwelling (1 Corinthians 3:16; 1 Peter 2:5).

verseByVerse.quote: In him you also are being built together into a dwelling place for God by the Spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God now lives among his people by his Spirit: the church is his home.

You also. Gentiles included.

Dwelling place. What the tabernacle and temple pictured is fulfilled in the gathered church.

For worship. When the church meets, God is at home. Come expecting him.

2.overview:
Chapter 2 tells the gospel twice. First as the story of every believer (vv. 1–10): we were dead in sin, ruled by the world, the devil and our own desires, and by nature under God’s wrath. “But God”, rich in mercy, made us alive with Christ, raised us and seated us with him, so that for ever he may display the riches of his grace. Salvation is entirely by grace through faith, God’s gift and not our achievement, and its fruit is a life of the good works God prepared for us.

Then as the story of two peoples (vv. 11–22). Gentiles were once outsiders, without Christ, without the covenants of promise, without hope and without God. Now, by Christ’s blood, they have been brought near. Christ himself is our peace: in his flesh he has torn down the wall of hostility between Jew and Gentile, ending the law’s regulations as a barrier, creating one new humanity and reconciling both to God in one body through the cross. Through him both have access to the Father by one Spirit. Gentile believers are no longer foreigners but fellow citizens and members of God’s household, built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets with Christ as cornerstone, growing into a holy temple where God lives by his Spirit.

3.title: The Mystery of Christ and the Fullness of God
3.text: <sup>1</sup>For this reason I, Paul, a prisoner of Christ Jesus on behalf of you Gentiles — <sup>2</sup>assuming that you have heard of the stewardship of God’s grace that was given to me for you, <sup>3</sup>how the mystery was made known to me by revelation, as I have written briefly. <sup>4</sup>When you read this, you can perceive my insight into the mystery of Christ, <sup>5</sup>which was not made known to the sons of men in other generations as it has now been revealed to his holy apostles and prophets by the Spirit. <sup>6</sup>This mystery is that the Gentiles are fellow heirs, members of the same body, and partakers of the promise in Christ Jesus through the gospel. <sup>7</sup>Of this gospel I was made a minister according to the gift of God’s grace, which was given me by the working of his power. <sup>8</sup>To me, though I am the very least of all the saints, this grace was given, to preach to the Gentiles the unsearchable riches of Christ, <sup>9</sup>and to bring to light for everyone what is the plan of the mystery hidden for ages in God, who created all things, <sup>10</sup>so that through the church the manifold wisdom of God might now be made known to the rulers and authorities in the heavenly places. <sup>11</sup>This was according to the eternal purpose that he has realized in Christ Jesus our Lord, <sup>12</sup>in whom we have boldness and access with confidence through our faith in him. <sup>13</sup>So I ask you not to lose heart over what I am suffering for you, which is your glory. <sup>14</sup>For this reason I bow my knees before the Father, <sup>15</sup>from whom every family in heaven and on earth is named, <sup>16</sup>that according to the riches of his glory he may grant you to be strengthened with power through his Spirit in your inner being, <sup>17</sup>so that Christ may dwell in your hearts through faith — that you, being rooted and grounded in love, <sup>18</sup>may have strength to comprehend with all the saints what is the breadth and length and height and depth, <sup>19</sup>and to know the love of Christ that surpasses knowledge, that you may be filled with all the fullness of God. <sup>20</sup>Now to him who is able to do far more abundantly than all that we ask or think, according to the power at work within us, <sup>21</sup>to him be glory in the church and in Christ Jesus throughout all generations, forever and ever. Amen.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul, a prisoner for the Gentiles, explains that God entrusted to him the administration of grace for them: the mystery revealed to him, which he has briefly described. In past generations it was not made known as it now has been by the Spirit to the apostles and prophets: through the gospel the Gentiles are co-heirs with Israel, members of one body and sharers in the promise in Christ. Paul became its servant by God’s gracious gift and power. Though the least of all God’s people, he was given grace to preach Christ’s boundless riches to the Gentiles and to make plain to all how this long-hidden mystery works out, so that through the church God’s manifold wisdom should now be shown to the heavenly rulers, according to his eternal purpose in Christ, in whom we approach God with freedom and confidence through faith. So they should not be discouraged by his sufferings for them, which are their glory.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Mystery Hidden and Revealed

The concept of "mystery" (mysterion) in Pauline theology is not something puzzling or obscure. It is a technical term for a secret previously hidden in God that has now been disclosed in the gospel. The mystery of Christ — the inclusion of the Gentiles as co-heirs — was not absent from the Old Testament, but it was not fully clear. It was there in the Abrahamic promise ("in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed," Genesis 12:3), in the prophets (Isaiah 49:6; 60:3), in the Psalms (Psalm 87; 96:3). But the full disclosure awaited the coming of Christ and the apostolic proclamation of the gospel.

This "already hidden, now revealed" pattern is the structure of all biblical revelation. The Old Testament is full of types, shadows, and partial disclosures that only become fully visible in the light of Christ. This is why the Reformers insisted on the unity of the two Testaments — they are one revelation progressively unfolding, not two contradictory religions. And it is why reading the Old Testament through the lens of Christ is not an imposition on the text but the fulfilment of its own internal logic. The mystery of the Gentiles was always there; the church is now living in the age of its full disclosure.

Paul's description of himself as "the very least of all the saints" (v.8) has been the theme of Reformed meditation on gospel humility. The man who had been the church's most zealous persecutor, who had dragged men and women to prison and consented to their deaths, now counts himself the least worthy recipient of the grace he proclaims. This is not false modesty; it is the grammar of genuine encounter with grace. The closer you are to Christ, the more clearly you see how far you fall short — and the more marvellous it becomes that grace extends even to you.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Paul describes his ministry as the proclamation of "the unsearchable riches of Christ" (v.8). The Greek word for "unsearchable" (anexichniastos) means literally "untraceable" — riches so vast that you cannot find their boundary, cannot trace their perimeter, cannot reach their end. To the Ephesian church, surrounded by the very traceable riches of Artemis and the mystery cults — gods who could be appeased, blessing that could be earned, secrets that could be unlocked for a price — Paul announces something of a different order entirely. The riches of Christ are boundless. They cannot be exhausted. The more you receive, the more remains to be given. No mystery religion could offer this.

Now: Paul is in prison when he writes this, and he explicitly tells the Ephesians not to lose heart because of his sufferings (v.13). The apostle who has been entrusted with the most glorious news in the universe is sitting in a Roman cell when he writes it. This is the pattern of the gospel: its glory travels in the most unlikely vessels. The imprisoned apostle, the persecuted church, the minority community that the world dismisses — these are the means through which the manifold wisdom of God is made known. When the church is most visibly weak, it is often doing its most significant cosmic work. The angels are watching — and what they see is the wisdom of God displayed in jars of clay.

verseByVerse.quote: For this reason I, Paul, a prisoner of Christ Jesus on behalf of you Gentiles—
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul starts to pray, but first must explain why he is in chains: he is a prisoner because of his mission to the Gentiles.

For this reason. Because Gentiles are now part of God’s temple (2:22). The prayer resumes at verse 14.

A prisoner of Christ Jesus. Not Rome’s, but Christ’s. Paul was arrested over the Gentile issue (Acts 21:28; 22:21–22).

On a Tuesday. Your hardest circumstances can be held, as Paul held his, under Christ’s sovereignty.
verseByVerse.note: Paul was imprisoned because of his mission to the Gentiles; he breaks off here and resumes in verse 14.

verseByVerse.quote: assuming that you have heard of the stewardship of God's grace that was given to me for you, how the mystery was made known to me by revelation,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul was entrusted with God’s grace for the Gentiles, and given the revelation of a mystery.

Stewardship. Oikonomia, the management of a household: Paul is a steward of grace, not its owner (1 Corinthians 4:1).

By revelation. Paul did not invent his gospel (Galatians 1:11–12).
verseByVerse.note: A stewardship is a trust given to a household manager.

verseByVerse.quote: as I have written briefly. When you read this, you can perceive my insight into the mystery of Christ,
verseByVerse.commentary:
What Paul has already written shows his understanding of the mystery of Christ.

When you read. The letter itself carries apostolic insight. Scripture is the place we meet it now.

verseByVerse.quote: The mystery of Christ, which was not made known to the sons of men in other generations as it has now been revealed to his holy apostles and prophets by the Spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The mystery was not revealed to earlier generations as fully as it now has been, by the Spirit, to Christ’s apostles and prophets.

Not made known as now. The Old Testament foretold blessing for the nations (Genesis 12:3; Isaiah 49:6), but not that they would be equal members of one body without becoming Jews.

Where Christians differ. Some dispensationalists see the church as a mystery entirely hidden from the Old Testament, a parenthesis in God’s plan for Israel. Covenant theology sees the church as the fulfilment of the promises, now more clearly revealed. Verdict: the word “as” implies partial earlier revelation; the church fulfils God’s promise to Abraham.

Apostles and prophets. The foundation of the church (2:20).

verseByVerse.quote: This mystery is that the Gentiles are fellow heirs, members of the same body, and partakers of the promise in Christ Jesus through the gospel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The mystery is that Gentiles are fellow heirs, fellow members and fellow sharers with Israel in Christ.

Three “fellow” words. In Greek, three compounds with syn: co-heirs, co-body, co-sharers. Full equality.

Through the gospel. Not by law or ancestry.

For worship. If you are a Gentile believer, you are a fellow heir of Abraham’s promises. Give thanks.

verseByVerse.quote: Of this gospel I was made a minister according to the gift of God’s grace, which was given me by the working of his power. To me, though I am the very least of all the saints, this grace was given, to preach to the Gentiles the unsearchable riches of Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul, the least of all the saints, was made a servant of this gospel by grace, to preach Christ’s unsearchable riches to the nations.

Minister. Diakonos, servant.

The very least. Paul coins a word: “leaster”. He never forgot he had persecuted the church (1 Corinthians 15:9; 1 Timothy 1:15).

Unsearchable riches. Riches that can never be fully explored.

On a Tuesday. God uses people who know they are unworthy. Your past does not disqualify you from serving.

verseByVerse.quote: and to bring to light for everyone what is the plan of the mystery hidden for ages in God, who created all things,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul’s task is to bring to light God’s plan, hidden for ages in the Creator himself.

Plan. Textual note. Later manuscripts read “fellowship” instead of “plan” (KJV), and add “by Jesus Christ” after “created all things”. Verdict: “plan” (oikonomia) is original, and the addition is a later expansion.

Who created all things. The plan of salvation belongs to the Creator, who purposed it from the beginning.

verseByVerse.quote: so that through the church the manifold wisdom of God might now be made known to the rulers and authorities in the heavenly places.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Through the church, God’s many-sided wisdom is put on display before the spiritual powers.

Through the church. The church is God’s showcase to the universe.

Manifold. Many-coloured, richly varied: a united people of every nation shows the beauty of God’s wisdom.

Rulers and authorities. Angelic and demonic powers (1:21; 6:12). They watch the church.

On a Tuesday. Your church’s unity across race, class and culture is a sermon preached to heaven. Guard it.

verseByVerse.quote: This was according to the eternal purpose that he has realized in Christ Jesus our Lord, in whom we have boldness and access with confidence through our faith in him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s eternal purpose is accomplished in Christ, in whom we can approach God boldly and confidently through faith.

Eternal purpose. The church is no afterthought.

Boldness and access. Freedom of speech and right of entry before God (2:18; Hebrews 4:16).

Through our faith in him. Or “through his faithfulness”. Verdict: the usual reading, faith in Christ, fits Paul’s usage here.

For worship. Approach God today with confidence, not timidity.

verseByVerse.quote: So I ask you not to lose heart over what I am suffering for you, which is your glory.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul’s sufferings for the Gentiles are not a reason to lose heart but a sign of their glory.

Your glory. Paul suffers for their sake; his chains show how much their salvation is worth.

On a Tuesday. Do not be discouraged when Christian leaders suffer. God is at work.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul kneels before the Father, from whom every family in heaven and on earth is named. He asks that, out of his glorious riches, God will strengthen them with power in their inner being through his Spirit, so that Christ may make his home in their hearts through faith. Rooted and established in love, may they have power with all God’s people to grasp how wide, long, high and deep Christ’s love is, and to know this love that surpasses knowledge, so that they may be filled with all the fullness of God. To him who can do immeasurably more than all we ask or imagine, by the power at work in us, be glory in the church and in Christ Jesus through all generations for ever.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Indwelling Christ and the Fullness of God

The prayer of Ephesians 3:14–21 reveals the goal of the Christian life with startling clarity: not moral improvement, not doctrinal accuracy, not even evangelistic fruitfulness — but the fullness of God. "Filled with all the fullness of God" (v.19) is a goal so vast it cannot be reached in a lifetime, which is precisely the point. The Christian life is not a project with a completion date; it is a journey into an infinity that perpetually exceeds the traveller. Paul set no limit to his desires for the Ephesians — he asked for the infinite, because the infinite is what God offers.

The means of this fullness is the indwelling of Christ. "That Christ may dwell in your hearts through faith" (v.17) — the verb "dwell" (katoikein) means to settle, to take up permanent residence, as opposed to merely passing through. This is not the occasional visitation of religious experience; it is the abiding presence of the living Christ in the interior life of the believer. The Reformers consistently emphasized that union with Christ — not merely forgiveness, not merely a changed record before God, but genuine, living union with the risen Lord — is the foundation of the entire Christian life. It is from this union that everything else flows: assurance, holiness, prayer, service, suffering, joy.

The doxology of vv.20–21 is also a theology of prayer. It teaches us that God is not limited by the smallness of our asking. The greatness of our petitions cannot exhaust his capacity to answer; the boldness of our faith cannot outrun his willingness to give. The God to whom we pray is the God who can do more than we can imagine asking — and the power by which he does it is "at work within us." It is the same resurrection power of Ephesians 1:19–20. Our prayers are small; his answers are not required to match them.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The mystery religions of Ephesus promised spiritual fullness — union with the divine, access to hidden power — through initiation, through ritual, through the gradual ascent of the initiated. The costs were significant: financial, social, sometimes physical. And the fullness promised was always partial, always provisional, always requiring the next level of initiation. Paul prays for his readers to receive a fullness that no mystery religion could offer and no initiation could achieve: the fullness of God himself, freely given, received through faith, sustained by the Spirit. The contrast with what Ephesus was selling could not have been more pointed.

Now: "Far more abundantly than all that we ask or think" — this phrase has stood as one of the great encouragements of Christian prayer across the centuries. When we pray small, God answers large. When we cannot find words, the Spirit intercedes. When the situation seems beyond recovery, we serve the God who raises the dead. The doxology of Ephesians 3 is not merely a liturgical flourish; it is a declaration of the character of the God to whom we pray. He exceeds our prayers not because he is indifferent to them but because he is inexhaustibly generous. Every time this doxology is spoken in corporate worship, the church is reminding itself — and the watching powers — of who their God is.

verseByVerse.quote: For this reason I bow my knees before the Father, from whom every family in heaven and on earth is named.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul kneels in prayer before the Father who gives every family its name.

Bow my knees. Jews usually prayed standing; kneeling shows deep earnestness (Luke 22:41).

The Father. Textual note. Later manuscripts add “of our Lord Jesus Christ” (KJV). Verdict: not original.

Every family. A wordplay: Father (patēr), family (patria). Every family, angelic and human, derives its existence and name from God.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “family” renders patria, a word closely related to “father” (pater) in verse 14.

verseByVerse.quote: That according to the riches of his glory he may grant you to be strengthened with power through his Spirit in your inner being.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul asks that the Spirit will strengthen them inwardly with power from God’s glorious riches.

According to his riches. Not out of them, but in proportion to them.

Inner being. The renewed self (2 Corinthians 4:16).

On a Tuesday. Pray for inner strength, not only for outward circumstances.

verseByVerse.quote: So that Christ may dwell in your hearts through faith, that you, being rooted and grounded in love.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The goal of inner strengthening is that Christ may be at home in their hearts through faith.

Dwell. Katoikeō, to settle down, make a home. Christ already lives in believers; Paul prays that he will be fully at home there.

Rooted and grounded. Pictures from plants and buildings: love as the soil and foundation.

verseByVerse.quote: may have strength to comprehend with all the saints what is the breadth and length and height and depth,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul prays that together with all believers they may grasp the immeasurable dimensions of Christ’s love.

With all the saints. We understand Christ’s love together, not alone.

Breadth, length, height, depth. Not measurements to calculate, but a way of saying it is boundless in every direction.

parallels.desc: higher than heaven, deeper than Sheol

verseByVerse.quote: and to know the love of Christ that surpasses knowledge, that you may be filled with all the fullness of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ’s love surpasses knowledge, yet can be known, and knowing it fills us with God’s fullness.

Know what surpasses knowledge. A deliberate paradox: we can know truly what we will never know fully.

Filled with all the fullness of God. Not becoming God, but being filled with all that God gives.

For worship. Ask God to show you more of Christ’s love today.

verseByVerse.quote: Now to him who is able to do far more abundantly than all that we ask or think, according to the power at work within us,
verseByVerse.commentary:
God is able to do far more than anything we can ask or even imagine, by the power already at work in us.

Far more abundantly. Paul invents a super-superlative.

All that we ask or think. God’s ability outruns our requests and our imagination.

What it does not mean. Not a promise to give whatever we imagine, but assurance that God’s purposes for us are greater than our dreams (Romans 8:28–32).

On a Tuesday. Pray bigger. And trust God when he answers differently from what you asked.

verseByVerse.quote: to him be glory in the church and in Christ Jesus throughout all generations, forever and ever. Amen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
All glory belongs to God, displayed in the church and in Christ, for ever.

In the church and in Christ Jesus. The body and the head together display God’s glory.

Throughout all generations. The church will outlast every empire.

For worship. Say the Amen aloud.

3.overview:
Paul begins to pray (v. 1), then breaks off to explain his own role in God’s plan (vv. 2–13). God gave him, a prisoner for the Gentiles’ sake, a stewardship of grace: the revelation of the mystery of Christ, hidden in earlier generations and now revealed by the Spirit to the apostles and prophets. The mystery is that Gentiles are fellow heirs with Israel, members of the same body and sharers in the promise through the gospel. Paul, the least of all the saints, was given the task of preaching Christ’s unsearchable riches to the nations, so that through the church God’s many-sided wisdom might be displayed to the powers in the heavenly places. His sufferings are for their glory, so they must not lose heart.

Then he resumes his prayer (vv. 14–21), kneeling before the Father from whom every family takes its name. He asks that they be strengthened by the Spirit in the inner person, that Christ may dwell in their hearts by faith, and that, rooted in love, they may grasp the immeasurable dimensions of Christ’s love that surpasses knowledge, and be filled with all the fullness of God. The chapter ends in a doxology to the God who can do far more than we ask or imagine, to whom be glory in the church and in Christ Jesus for ever.

4.title: Unity, Gifts, and the New Self

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — Walk Worthy: The Unity of the Spirit
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: As a prisoner for the Lord, Paul urges them to live worthy of their calling: completely humble and gentle, patient, bearing with one another in love, and working hard to keep the unity the Spirit gives through the bond of peace. There is one body and one Spirit, one hope, one Lord, one faith, one baptism, and one God and Father of all, over all, through all and in all.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Unity of the Church as Theological Reality

The passage reveals that the unity of the church is not an aspiration or a programme — it is an ontological reality that precedes and grounds every effort to express it. The Spirit has already created one body. The question is not whether unity exists but whether our behaviour honours the unity that does. This distinction between the given reality and the required response is characteristic of Paul's ethical method throughout the letter: indicative first, imperative second. Be what you are. Express what is already true.

The four virtues through which unity is maintained — humility, gentleness, patience, forbearance — are a portrait of Christlike character applied to community life. They are not soft virtues; they are demanding ones. Humility means thinking of others' interests above your own (Philippians 2:3). Gentleness (prautēs) belongs to the word Jesus used of himself (“I am gentle and lowly in heart,” Matthew 11:29) — strength in service of love. Patience is the willingness to absorb rather than retaliate. Forbearance is the daily choice to keep choosing the person in front of you rather than withdrawing when they disappoint. Together these virtues create the environment in which the given unity of the Spirit can be made visible.

The Reformers consistently emphasised that doctrinal unity and relational unity are inseparable. The sevenfold “one” of vv.4–6 grounds the relational unity of vv.2–3 in doctrinal reality. We are not called to unity by ignoring our differences or pretending that doctrine doesn't matter. We are called to unity because there is genuinely one Lord, one faith, one baptism — and the body that confesses these things is, by that very confession, one. Preserving this unity is not sentimentality; it is theological faithfulness.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Ephesian church was the most socially diverse community in the city. Former Artemis worshippers, Jewish converts, Greek philosophers, slaves and freedmen, wealthy merchants and harbour workers — all brought together by the preaching of the gospel. The centrifugal forces were enormous. Every human instinct would have been to fracture along existing social fault lines. Paul's “therefore” connects the unity he calls for directly to the cosmic reality of chapter 2: the wall has already come down. The body is already one. Now: walk like it. Bear with one another. Choose the humility that makes room for people unlike you. This was not a small ask in first-century Ephesus.

Now: The church in our age is under intense pressure to fragment — along political lines, cultural lines, worship-style lines, theological nuance lines. The market logic of contemporary Christianity encourages us to shop for churches that suit our preferences, reinforcing the very homogeneity that Paul's vision challenges. Against this, Ephesians 4:1–6 calls the church to a costly unity rooted not in shared preference but in shared confession: one Lord, one faith, one baptism. The local church that perseveres through its internal differences — that chooses patient, humble, forbearing love over the easier path of fragmentation — is doing something more theologically significant than it knows. It is bearing witness to the one God who is over all and through all and in all.

verseByVerse.quote: I therefore, a prisoner for the Lord, urge you to walk in a manner worthy of the calling to which you have been called.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Doctrine leads to duty: those called by God must live a life that matches their calling.

Therefore. The hinge of the letter. Chapters 1–3 are indicative (what God has done); chapters 4–6 imperative (how to live).

Walk. Paul’s word for the whole way of life (2:2, 10; 4:17; 5:2, 8, 15).

The calling. God’s effective summons into Christ and his people (1:18; Romans 8:30): to be holy and blameless (1:4).

A prisoner for the Lord. Paul writes from chains: the call costs, and he has paid.

Worthy. Of equal weight: your conduct should balance your calling. Not to earn it, but to fit it.
verseByVerse.note: Chapters 1–3 set out what God has done; chapters 4–6 show the life that follows.

verseByVerse.quote: With all humility and gentleness, with patience, bearing with one another in love.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The worthy life is marked first by humility, gentleness and patient love, the virtues that keep a church together.

Humility. A word Greeks used for servility; Christ made it a virtue (Philippians 2:3–8).

Gentleness. Strength under control (Matthew 11:29).

Bearing with one another. Patience with people who annoy us, and whom we annoy.

On a Tuesday. Think of the believer who irritates you most. Bear with them today in love.

verseByVerse.quote: Eager to maintain the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christians do not create unity; the Spirit has given it, and they must eagerly guard it.

Eager. Make every effort: unity takes work.

The unity of the Spirit. Already given (2:14–18).

The bond of peace. Peace is the cord that ties believers together.

What it does not mean. Not unity at the cost of truth (v. 13–15) or a single church organisation. It is the shared life of all who belong to Christ, kept by humility and patience.

verseByVerse.quote: There is one body and one Spirit — just as you were called to the one hope that belongs to your call — one Lord, one faith, one baptism,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christian unity rests on seven great realities that all believers share.

One body. One church, though many congregations.
