One Spirit, one Lord, one God. The Trinity is the foundation of the church’s unity.

One faith. The shared content of the gospel.

One baptism. The common sign of entry into Christ. Where Christians differ. Christians disagree on the subjects and mode of baptism, and many churches do not recognise one another’s baptism. Verdict: the app’s credobaptist view, held charitably: believers’ baptism best fits the New Testament, but paedobaptist Christians are brothers and sisters in the one faith and the one body.

verseByVerse.quote: one God and Father of all, who is over all and through all and in all.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Above all and through all and in all is the one God and Father.

Of all. Of all believers, his family (3:15).

Over, through, in. God’s transcendence, providence and presence.

Textual note. Later manuscripts add “you” (in you all, KJV) or “us”. Verdict: the shorter text is original.

For worship. Worship the one God whom the whole church worships with you.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Each believer has received grace as Christ apportioned it. As the psalm says, the conqueror ascended with captives and gave gifts to people; the one who ascended first descended, and he ascended above the heavens to fill everything. He gave apostles, prophets, evangelists, and pastors and teachers, to equip his people for service and build up his body, until all reach unity in faith and knowledge of the Son, maturity and the full stature of Christ. Then we will no longer be like children tossed by every wind of teaching and human trickery, but, speaking the truth in love, will grow in every way into Christ, the head, from whom the whole body, joined and held together, builds itself up in love as each part does its work.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Ascended Christ and the Equipping Ministry

The passage grounds all ministry in the ascension of Christ — a movement of Pauline theology that is often underemphasised. It is the ascended Christ who gives gifts to his church. The one who has “ascended far above all the heavens” (v.10) is also the one who “fills all things” — present everywhere, sovereign over all, distributing gifts according to his wisdom and his grace. Ministry is not primarily a human enterprise; it is a dimension of the ongoing, active reign of the risen and ascended King.

The list of gifted persons — apostles, prophets, evangelists, shepherds and teachers — has generated significant debate about which offices are permanent and which ceased with the apostolic age. The Reformed tradition has consistently held that the foundational offices (apostles and prophets, Ephesians 2:20) were unique to the founding of the church, while the equipping offices (evangelists, pastor-teachers) continue throughout the church's history. What remains constant in every age is the purpose: equipping the saints for ministry until the whole body reaches the fullness of Christ.

The metaphor of the body in vv.15–16 is Paul's most developed statement of mutual ministry. The body grows “when each part is working properly” — not when a few parts are exceptionally active while the rest remain passive, but when every member is fulfilling their function. This is the vision of a church in which every person is a minister — not because every person preaches, but because every person contributes the grace-gift they have received to the building up of the whole. The body that achieves this grows toward Christ in every way. The body that fails at this — where a few do everything and the many receive — stunts its own growth.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Ephesian church had known extraordinary leadership — Paul himself had spent three years there, and the elders he had appointed knew the weight of shepherding a flock in a hostile city (Acts 20:28–31). Now Paul is gone, and his letter is itself an act of equipping: preparing the church to continue faithfully without his physical presence. The gifted leaders he describes in vv.11–12 are, in the first instance, the elders and teachers of the Ephesian church — men charged with the immense responsibility of preparing every member for a ministry that would build the body in Paul's absence. This was not a programme; it was a pastoral theology applied to a real community facing real challenges.

Now: The consumer church — where the congregation pays for spiritual services delivered by professional clergy — is the precise opposite of Paul's vision. It produces spiritual infants who cannot feed themselves, who are vulnerable to every wind of doctrine, who have no sense of their own giftedness or their own call to ministry. The equipping church — where gifted leaders deliberately, systematically invest in the ministry capacity of every member — produces a body that is robust, maturing, and growing in love. The question for every church leader is not “How well am I performing?” but “How well am I equipping?” And the question for every member is not “Am I being fed?” but “Am I contributing?”

verseByVerse.quote: But grace was given to each one of us according to the measure of Christ’s gift.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Within the church’s unity, Christ has given every believer a measure of grace for serving.

Each one of us. No believer is giftless (1 Corinthians 12:7; 1 Peter 4:10).

The measure of Christ’s gift. Christ decides the gift and its size.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore it says, 'When he ascended on high he led a host of captives, and he gave gifts to men.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The ascended Christ, like a conquering king, shares the spoils of his victory with his people.

Psalm 68:18. God ascends Zion as victor, leading captives and receiving gifts. Paul reads “gave” rather than “received”, following a Jewish interpretation (the Aramaic Targum) and the sense of the psalm: a conqueror receives tribute in order to distribute it.

A host of captives. Christ’s defeated enemies, sin, death and Satan, paraded in his triumph (Colossians 2:15); some read it of those he has freed.

Gifts to men. The gifts are named in v. 11: people given to the church.
verseByVerse.note: The psalm pictures God ascending Mount Zion in victory, receiving tribute; Paul applies it to Christ, who in triumph gives gifts. A Jewish Aramaic paraphrase of the psalm also reads “gave gifts.”

parallels.desc: you ascended on high, leading a host of captives

verseByVerse.quote: (In saying, 'He ascended,' what does it mean but that he had also descended into the lower regions, the earth? He who descended is the one who also ascended far above all the heavens, that he might fill all things.)
verseByVerse.commentary:
The one who ascended had first descended, and now fills the whole universe.

Lower regions. Where Christians differ. Some read this as Christ’s descent into hell between his death and resurrection (compare the Apostles’ Creed). Most interpreters read “the lower regions, the earth”: his incarnation, coming down to earth (John 3:13). Others suggest the Spirit’s descent at Pentecost. Verdict: the incarnation, and his humiliation to death and the grave.

Textual note. Later manuscripts add “first” (descended first). Verdict: an interpretative addition.

That he might fill all things. His exaltation fills creation with his rule.
verseByVerse.note: “The lower regions, the earth” may mean his coming down to earth in the incarnation.

verseByVerse.quote: And he gave the apostles, the prophets, the evangelists, the shepherds and teachers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ’s gifts to the church include gifted people: apostles, prophets, evangelists, and shepherds who teach.

Apostles and prophets. The foundational gifts (2:20; 3:5). Where Christians differ. Some churches recognise apostles and prophets today. Cessationists hold that these foundational offices ended with the apostolic age, though missionaries and preachers continue similar work. Verdict: the app’s cessationist view, held charitably: no one today holds the apostles’ authority, and the prophetic foundation is complete in Scripture.

Evangelists. Those gifted to take the gospel to new places (Acts 21:8; 2 Timothy 4:5).

Shepherds and teachers. Probably one office: pastors who teach, the elders (Acts 20:28; 1 Peter 5:2).
verseByVerse.note: “Shepherds” is the word often translated “pastors.”

verseByVerse.quote: to equip the saints for the work of ministry, for building up the body of Christ,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Church leaders exist not to do all the ministry but to equip all God’s people for it.

To equip. Katartismos, to mend nets, set bones, train and fit out.

The saints. All believers.

The work of ministry. Service, done by the whole church.

On a Tuesday. What ministry has God equipped you for? Ask your elders, and use it.

verseByVerse.quote: until we all attain to the unity of the faith and of the knowledge of the Son of God, to mature manhood, to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ, so that we may no longer be children, tossed to and fro by the waves and carried about by every wind of doctrine, by human cunning, by craftiness in deceitful schemes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The goal of ministry is a mature church, grown up into Christ and no longer tossed about by false teaching.

Unity of the faith. Shared truth, not lowest-common-denominator agreement.

Mature manhood. Adult faith, measured by Christ himself.

Children tossed. Immature believers chase every new idea and fall prey to clever deceivers.

On a Tuesday. If every new trend in Christian books or online preachers moves you, ask for grounding in the whole counsel of God.

verseByVerse.quote: Rather, speaking the truth in love, we are to grow up in every way into him who is the head, into Christ, from whom the whole body, joined and held together by every joint with which it is equipped, when each part is working properly, makes the body grow so that it builds itself up in love.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Truth spoken in love makes the whole body grow up into Christ, its head, as every part does its work.

Speaking the truth in love. Truth without love is harsh; love without truth is empty.

From whom. Growth comes from the head and flows through every member.

Each part. Every member matters.

For worship. Thank Christ for the members of his body who have helped you grow.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–24 — Put Off the Old, Put On the New
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul insists they must stop living like unbelieving Gentiles, whose thinking is futile, whose understanding is darkened, and who are cut off from God’s life by ignorance and hardened hearts; having lost all sensitivity, they give themselves to sensuality and every kind of impurity. That is not how they came to know Christ, if they truly heard and were taught the truth that is in Jesus: to put off the old self, corrupted by deceitful desires, to be renewed in their minds, and to put on the new self, created to be like God in true righteousness and holiness.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Renewal of the Mind and the New Humanity

The “old self” and “new self” of this passage are not psychological categories — they are eschatological ones. The old self is the Adamic humanity: the self that has inherited Adam's corruption, lives under the dominion of sin, and is “corrupt through deceitful desires” (v.22). The new self is the new humanity created in Christ — what Paul elsewhere calls “the last Adam” (1 Corinthians 15:45). To be “in Christ” is to have been transferred from the old humanity to the new, from the domain of the first Adam to the domain of the Second.

The renewing of the mind (v.23) is the cognitive dimension of this transfer. Romans 12:2 makes the same point: “be transformed by the renewal of your mind.” The mind that has been shaped by the world — its values, its assumptions, its desires — must be reshaped by the word and Spirit of God. This is not achieved in a moment; it is the work of a lifetime. Every act of sustained Bible meditation, every time truth displaces a lie, every time a Spirit-given desire overcomes a flesh-driven one, the mind is being renewed. This is the slow and glorious work of sanctification.

The goal of the renewal is “the likeness of God in true righteousness and holiness” (v.24). This is the restoration of the image of God that was defaced at the fall. God made humanity in his image; sin corrupted that image; Christ has come to restore it. The new self is not merely morally better than the old — it is ontologically different, created anew after the very likeness of God. This is why the Christian life is not ultimately about rule-keeping but about becoming who you already are in Christ: the image-bearer of God, restored and renewed.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Ephesus was a city of extraordinary sensual abundance. The temple complex of Artemis, the bath-houses, the theatre, the commercial district — pleasure was available in every form and at every price. To be a Christian in Ephesus was to swim against a powerful and relentless current. Paul does not tell the Ephesian Christians to try harder or to exercise greater willpower. He gives them something more powerful: a new identity. You are not the old self anymore. The garment of the old life is to be put off — not held on to, not worn occasionally for old time's sake, but removed and discarded. And in its place: the new self, created after God's own likeness.

Now: The pornified, entertainment-saturated, hyper-stimulated culture of the 21st century is Ephesus with better technology. The mechanisms of desire-manipulation are more sophisticated; the availability of darkness is more immediate; the cultural current against a holy life runs faster. Paul's answer is unchanged and still the most powerful available: not more discipline applied to the old self, but the daily renewal of the mind in the truth of the gospel — who you are in Christ, what you have been given, who you are becoming. The Christian who meditates daily on Scripture, who submits their thinking to the word of God, who asks the Spirit to renew their mind — this person is not swimming against the current on their own. They are being transformed.

verseByVerse.quote: Now this I say and testify in the Lord, that you must no longer walk as the Gentiles do, in the futility of their minds.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Believers must no longer live the way the unbelieving world lives, with minds that come to nothing.

Testify in the Lord. A solemn charge.

The Gentiles. Here, unbelievers; the readers were Gentiles by birth but are now God’s people.

Futility. Emptiness, purposelessness (Romans 1:21).

verseByVerse.quote: They are darkened in their understanding, alienated from the life of God because of the ignorance that is in them, due to their hardness of heart. They have become callous and have given themselves up to sensuality, greedy to practice every kind of impurity.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Unbelief begins with a hardened heart, which darkens the mind and leads to self-abandonment to impurity.

The order. Hardness of heart produces ignorance, ignorance alienation from God’s life, and these lead to callousness and sensuality.

Callous. Past feeling: the conscience grows numb.

Sensuality. Aselgeia: shameless indulgence that no longer hides or blushes.

Greedy to practise impurity. The same “wanting more” as covetousness (5:3): appetite that is never satisfied.

Gave themselves up. Compare Romans 1:24: God gave them up; here they give themselves up.

On a Tuesday. Repeated sin numbs the conscience. Do not trust the fact that something no longer feels wrong.

verseByVerse.quote: But that is not the way you learned Christ!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ himself is the curriculum, and he does not teach that way of life.

Learned Christ. Not just learned about him: they learned him.

verseByVerse.quote: assuming that you have heard about him and were taught in him, as the truth is in Jesus,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Truth is found in Jesus, and believers have been taught by him.

Heard him, taught in him. Christ speaks through the apostolic gospel.

The truth is in Jesus. The only time Paul uses the name “Jesus” alone in Ephesians: the truth is in the historical person.

verseByVerse.quote: to put off your old self, which belongs to your former manner of life and is corrupt through deceitful desires,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Conversion means taking off the old self like filthy clothing.

Put off. Like clothes. The old self, who we were in Adam, has been crucified with Christ (Romans 6:6); now we must live it out.

Corrupt. Decaying, rotting from within.

Deceitful desires. Sin always promises more than it gives.
verseByVerse.note: The “old self” (literally “old man”) is the person we were in Adam, before union with Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: and to be renewed in the spirit of your minds,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Change begins in the mind, continually renewed by God.

Renewed. Present tense and passive: an ongoing work God does in us (Romans 12:2).

The spirit of your minds. The inner attitude that steers your thinking: your outlook, not just your opinions.

On a Tuesday. What you fill your mind with shapes who you become. Feed it with Scripture.

verseByVerse.quote: and to put on the new self, created after the likeness of God in true righteousness and holiness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Believers must put on the new self, created to be like God in true righteousness and holiness.

Created. The new self is God’s new creation (2:10), restoring the image of God (Colossians 3:10; Genesis 1:27).

True. Righteousness and holiness that come from the truth.

For worship. Thank God that he is remaking you in his likeness.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: So they must stop lying and speak truthfully to one another, for they are members of one body. In anger they must not sin, nor let anger outlast the day and give the devil a foothold. Thieves must stop stealing and work honestly, so as to have something to share with those in need. No unwholesome talk should come from their mouths, only what builds others up and gives grace to those who hear. They must not grieve the Holy Spirit, with whom they were sealed for the day of redemption. They must get rid of bitterness, rage, anger, brawling, slander and malice, and be kind and compassionate, forgiving one another as God forgave them in Christ.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Grieving of the Spirit and the Ethics of Grace

Verse 30 — “do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God, by whom you were sealed for the day of redemption” — is one of the most searching statements in the New Testament about the nature of the Spirit. He can be grieved. The Holy Spirit is not an impersonal force that responds mechanically to human sin; he is a Person with genuine emotional sensibility who is affected by the moral life of the community he inhabits. The sins Paul has listed — falsehood, uncontrolled anger, stealing, corrupting speech, bitterness, wrath, malice — do not merely harm the community; they wound the indwelling Guest.

The phrase “by whom you were sealed for the day of redemption” provides the context for the warning. The Spirit who can be grieved is the same Spirit who has sealed us for the final day — who is our guarantee of the inheritance (1:14), the deposit of our future glory. To grieve him is therefore not a trivial matter; it is to harm the very relationship that is the ground of our assurance and the means of our transformation. This is not a threat to the believer's salvation; Paul does not say “by whom you were sealed unless you grieve him.” The sealing is certain. But the quality of the Spirit's presence and work in the community is affected by how the community lives.

The climactic command — “forgive one another, as God in Christ forgave you” (v.32) — sets the standard for Christian forgiveness at the level of the cross: freely given, fully extended, without conditions. The Reformers consistently emphasised that forgiveness is not a feeling but a decision — the decision to release the debt, to no longer hold the offence against the offender, to treat them as God treats us in Christ: with kindness and grace. This is impossible from human resources. It is possible only for those who have received it from God and draw on the same source to extend it to others.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Ephesian church was extraordinarily diverse. With diversity comes friction. The command against falsehood (v.25) — “speak truth with your neighbour, for we are members of one another” — addresses the social lubricant of deception that holds many human communities together. In the body of Christ, truth-telling is not optional; it is structurally necessary. A body in which the members lie to one another cannot function. The command against corrupting speech (v.29) — only what builds up — addresses the tongue that tears down, the word that diminishes, the comment that cuts. In a diverse community under pressure, these are the sins most likely to do lasting damage.

Now: “Do not let the sun go down on your anger” is one of the most practically demanding commands in Scripture, and one of the most consistently violated in married life, family life, and church life. We carry grievances. We nurse wounds. We let distance harden into walls. The apostle's word cuts through all of it: move toward resolution before night falls.

This does not mean every conflict is resolved in an evening — some wounds take weeks of patient, humble work to heal. But the direction must always be toward each other, not away. The community that actually practices this — that refuses to let resentment calcify, that keeps short accounts, that forgives as God in Christ forgave — will be noticed. It will be extraordinary. It will be a sign of the Kingdom.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, having put away falsehood, let each one of you speak the truth with his neighbour.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because believers belong to one another, lying has no place among them.

Speak the truth. Zechariah 8:16.

Members of one another. Lying to a fellow believer is like the hand deceiving the eye.

On a Tuesday. Watch for small lies: exaggeration, flattery, excuses.

parallels.desc: speak the truth to one another

verseByVerse.quote: Be angry and do not sin; do not let the sun go down on your anger,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Anger can be right, but it must not lead to sin or be nursed overnight.

Be angry and do not sin. Psalm 4:4. There is righteous anger at evil (Mark 3:5), but most of our anger is wounded pride (James 1:20).

Before sunset. Deal with it quickly; reconcile the same day if you can.

What it does not mean. Not a command to be angry, nor permission for rage.

parallels.desc: be angry, and do not sin

verseByVerse.quote: and give no opportunity to the devil.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nursed anger gives the devil a foothold in the heart and in the church.

Opportunity. Topos, a place, a foothold.

On a Tuesday. Resentment you keep for weeks is ground you have handed to the enemy. Take it back.

verseByVerse.quote: Let the thief no longer steal, but rather let him labour, doing honest work with his own hands, so that he may have something to share with anyone in need.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The thief must become a worker, and the worker a giver: grace turns taking into sharing.

Labour. Honest, even manual work is honourable.

What it does not mean. Not that earning well or saving is suspect. Paul assumes work produces more than you need; the question is what you do with the surplus.

To share. The goal of work is not only self-support but generosity.

On a Tuesday. Theft includes padding expenses, idle hours on paid time, and unpaid debts. And plan to give from what you earn.

verseByVerse.quote: Let no corrupting talk come out of your mouths, but only such as is good for building up, as fits the occasion, that it may give grace to those who hear.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christian speech must build others up and give grace to those who hear.

Corrupting. Rotten, like decaying fruit: gossip, crude jokes, cutting remarks.

Fits the occasion. The right word at the right time (Proverbs 25:11).

Give grace. Words can be channels of God’s grace.

On a Tuesday. Before you post, send or say it, ask: will this build up?

verseByVerse.quote: And do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God, by whom you were sealed for the day of redemption.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sinful words and actions grieve the Holy Spirit, a person who loves us and has sealed us for redemption.

Grieve. Only a person can be grieved: the Spirit is not a force.

Sealed. God’s mark of ownership (1:13). Not a threat of losing salvation, but an appeal to love.
verseByVerse.note: A seal marked ownership and security until delivery.

parallels.desc: they rebelled and grieved his Holy Spirit

verseByVerse.quote: Let all bitterness and wrath and anger and clamour and slander be put away from you, along with all malice.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Every form of bitterness, rage and malice must be put away.

Bitterness. Resentment kept and fed. Wrath and anger. Sudden outbursts and settled anger. Clamour. Shouting. Slander. Speech that damages another’s name. Malice. Wishing harm.

The list. From inner bitterness, through outbursts, to shouting and slander, to settled malice: the progression of unchecked resentment.

verseByVerse.quote: Be kind to one another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, as God in Christ forgave you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Believers must be kind, tender and forgiving, because God in Christ has forgiven them.

Kind. Useful, generous goodness. Tenderhearted. Compassionate from the gut.

As God forgave you. The measure and the motive (Matthew 18:21–35; Colossians 3:13).

What it does not mean. Forgiveness does not mean pretending wrong was not wrong, nor always restoring trust immediately, nor removing just consequences; it means releasing the debt and refusing revenge.

On a Tuesday. Who do you need to forgive today?

For worship. Thank God for all he has forgiven you in Christ.

4.theology:
Ephesians 4 stakes out the great Reformed doctrine of the inseparability of justification and sanctification. The same grace that declares the sinner righteous also begins to make them righteous. Not simultaneously, not automatically — but inevitably. Where the root is real, the fruit will come. Paul’s commands in this chapter are not the conditions of acceptance; they are the evidence of it. The indicative always precedes and grounds the imperative.

The chapter also gives the church its most searching doctrine of common life. The body of Christ is not a collection of private spiritual journeys happening in the same building. It is an organism, with every member genuinely joined to every other — responsible for each other’s growth, dependent on each other’s gifts, harmed by each other’s sin. Falsehood in the body is not a private failure; it is a systemic wound. Unresolved anger is not a personal problem; it is a strategic opening for the enemy. This is the doctrine of the church made viscerally practical.

And at the centre stands the renewal of the mind — the hinge on which all change turns. Not willpower, not behaviour management, but transformation at the level where thinking happens. This is the Spirit’s sovereign work, received through the ordinary means of grace: the word, prayer, honest community, and obedience to what is already known. The Christian does not renew themselves. But they can position themselves daily in the hands of the One who does. cf. Rom. 12:1–2; 2 Cor. 3:18; Phil. 2:12–13.
4.examples:
Then: The Ephesian believers had come out of a culture saturated with the very patterns Paul describes in vv. 17–19 — a world of mystery religions, sexual licence, and moral relativism where the only sin was public embarrassment. To be told to “put off” this was not a minor adjustment; it was a complete reorientation of identity. And the alternative Paul offered — speaking truth, controlling anger, working honestly, forgiving freely — would have looked countercultural to the point of strangeness. The church in Ephesus was being asked to be a visible sign that a different humanity was possible.

Now: The culture has changed; the pressure has not. The same patterns Paul named are alive and well: the mind drifting, the conscience growing quieter, the appetite demanding more. The same temptations assault the same pressure points: to manage rather than truth-tell, to nurse grievance rather than forgive, to speak what entertains rather than what builds. And the same command stands: no longer walk as those who do not know God. Not because you must earn your standing — that is secured in Christ — but because you have been made new, and new creatures do not live in the old way.

You, reading this chapter on a Monday morning, can take one thing to work: the person sitting across from you is either a fellow member of the body or a neighbour made in God’s image. Either way, what you say matters, what you do with your anger matters, how you handle the truth matters. The renewal of the mind is not a mystical event. It is what happens when the Christian opens the Bible instead of the phone, prays instead of broods, speaks the honest word instead of the comfortable one — and does it again tomorrow. This is how the body builds itself up in love.
4.overview:
With chapter 4 Ephesians turns from what God has done (chapters 1–3) to how his people must live (chapters 4–6). The first call is to walk worthy of their calling, in humility, gentleness and patient love, keeping the unity the Spirit has created, for there is one body, one Spirit, one hope, one Lord, one faith, one baptism and one God and Father of all. Within that unity, the ascended Christ has given gifts to each believer, and has given the church apostles, prophets, evangelists and shepherd-teachers to equip all God’s people for ministry, until the whole body reaches maturity, no longer tossed about by false teaching, but speaking the truth in love and growing up into Christ the head.

Then Paul describes the new life. Believers must no longer live like the Gentiles, darkened in understanding and hardened in heart, given over to impurity. That is not how they learned Christ. They have been taught to put off the old self, be renewed in mind, and put on the new self, created to be like God in righteousness and holiness. The chapter ends with practical examples: truthfulness, anger without sin, honest work that enables giving, speech that builds up, and the kindness and forgiveness that mirror God’s forgiveness in Christ, so as not to grieve the Holy Spirit.

5.title: Walking in Love and the Mystery of Marriage
5.text: <sup>1</sup>Therefore be imitators of God, as beloved children. <sup>2</sup>And walk in love, as Christ loved us and gave himself up for us, a fragrant offering and sacrifice to God. <sup>3</sup>But sexual immorality and all impurity or covetousness must not even be named among you, as is proper among saints. <sup>4</sup>Let there be no filthiness nor foolish talk nor crude joking, which are out of place, but instead let there be thanksgiving. <sup>5</sup>For you may be sure of this, that everyone who is sexually immoral or impure, or who is covetous (that is, an idolater), has no inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and God. <sup>6</sup>Let no one deceive you with empty words, for because of these things the wrath of God comes upon the sons of disobedience. <sup>7</sup>Therefore do not become partners with them; <sup>8</sup>for at one time you were darkness, but now you are light in the Lord. Walk as children of light <sup>9</sup>(for the fruit of light is found in all that is good and right and true), <sup>10</sup>and try to discern what is pleasing to the Lord. <sup>11</sup>Take no part in the unfruitful works of darkness, but instead expose them. <sup>12</sup>For it is shameful even to speak of the things that they do in secret. <sup>13</sup>But when anything is exposed by the light, it becomes visible, <sup>14</sup>for anything that becomes visible is light. Therefore it says, “Awake, O sleeper, and arise from the dead, and Christ will shine on you.” <sup>15</sup>Look carefully then how you walk, not as unwise but as wise, <sup>16</sup>making the best use of the time, because the days are evil. <sup>17</sup>Therefore do not be foolish, but understand what the will of the Lord is. <sup>18</sup>And do not get drunk with wine, for that is debauchery, but be filled with the Spirit, <sup>19</sup>addressing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing and making melody to the Lord with your heart, <sup>20</sup>giving thanks always and for everything to God the Father in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, <sup>21</sup>submitting to one another out of reverence for Christ. <sup>22</sup>Wives, submit to your own husbands, as to the Lord. <sup>23</sup>For the husband is the head of the wife even as Christ is the head of the church, his body, and is himself its Savior. <sup>24</sup>Now as the church submits to Christ, so also wives should submit in everything to their husbands. <sup>25</sup>Husbands, love your wives, as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her, <sup>26</sup>that he might sanctify her, having cleansed her by the washing of water with the word, <sup>27</sup>so that he might present the church to himself in splendor, without spot or wrinkle or any such thing, that she might be holy and without blemish. <sup>28</sup>In the same way husbands should love their wives as their own bodies. He who loves his wife loves himself. <sup>29</sup>For no one ever hated his own flesh, but nourishes and cherishes it, just as Christ does the church, <sup>30</sup>because we are members of his body. <sup>31</sup>“Therefore a man shall leave his father and mother and hold fast to his wife, and the two shall become one flesh.” <sup>32</sup>This mystery is profound, and I am saying that it refers to Christ and the church. <sup>33</sup>However, let each one of you love his wife as himself, and let the wife see that she respects her husband.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: As God’s dearly loved children, they must imitate him and live a life of love, following Christ, who loved us and gave himself as a fragrant offering and sacrifice to God. Among God’s holy people there must be not even a hint of sexual immorality, impurity or greed, nor obscenity, foolish talk or coarse joking, which are out of place; instead there should be thanksgiving. No immoral, impure or greedy person, which is idolatry, has any inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and of God. They must not be deceived by empty words, for these things bring God’s wrath on the disobedient, so they must not share in them.
verseByVerse.theology:
Cruciform Love as the Pattern of the Christian Life

“A fragrant offering and sacrifice to God” (v.2) — Paul's description of Christ's self-giving at the cross is drawn directly from the Old Testament sacrificial language. The burnt offering was described as “a pleasing aroma to the LORD” (Leviticus 1:9; 8:21) — a sacrifice that God receives with satisfaction, that expresses the proper worship of creature before Creator. Paul applies this language to the cross: the death of Christ was the ultimate sacrifice, the perfect offering, the worship that satisfied the holiness of God and secured the salvation of his people.

The implication for ethics is profound: to walk in love in imitation of Christ is to participate in a form of worship. Every act of genuine, self-giving love — every moment of costly service, every forgiveness extended at personal cost, every preference of another's need over one's own comfort — is offered to God as a fragrant offering. The Christian life is not divided into sacred acts (prayer, church attendance) and secular acts (daily life, work, relationships). All of it is worship. The love that looks like Calvary, lived out in the ordinary texture of daily life, is received by God as the aroma of Christ himself.

Covetousness is identified in v.5 as idolatry — a striking identification that requires reflection. Covetousness is not merely wanting what others have; it is the orientation of the heart toward things rather than toward God, treating the creature as the source of satisfaction rather than the Creator. In this sense it is the root of sexual immorality as well: the sexualised culture is a culture of covetousness, of insatiable appetite, of treating persons as objects to be consumed. The gospel addresses this at the root by offering the only love that actually satisfies — the love of God in Christ, which surpasses knowledge and fills us with all the fullness of God (3:19).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: “Be imitators of God” — in the Greco-Roman world, this language had a specific resonance. The philosophical schools spoke of likeness to God as the goal of the spiritual life. But the path they offered was typically ascetic withdrawal, esoteric knowledge, ritual elevation. Paul offers a radically different path: imitate the God who descended, who gave himself up, who went to the cross for his enemies. The divine pattern to be imitated is not the god on the Olympian heights, remote and powerful, but the God who came down in love and poured himself out in death. The imitation called for is not upward escape but downward love.

Now: Sexual immorality has been rebranded in our age as liberation, as authentic self-expression, as the natural pursuit of desire. Covetousness is marketed as aspiration, ambition, the engine of economic progress. Paul's gospel cuts through all of it — not with a longer list of prohibitions, but with a higher vision. You are a beloved child of the God who gave his Son for you. You have been loved with a love that went to the cross. Now walk in that love: freely, lavishly, cruciformly, without counting the cost. This is not the moralism of a killjoy god; it is the invitation of a Father who wants his children to look like him and to know the joy of doing so.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore be imitators of God, as beloved children.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Children copy their father; God’s children must copy God.

Imitators. Mimētai, mimics. The only place in the New Testament where we are told to imitate God directly (compare Matthew 5:48).

Beloved children. We imitate him because we are loved, not to be loved.

On a Tuesday. How would your Father treat the people you will meet today? Do likewise.

verseByVerse.quote: And walk in love, as Christ loved us and gave himself up for us, a fragrant offering and sacrifice to God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The pattern of Christian love is Christ’s self-giving sacrifice.

Walk in love. Love as a way of life, not an occasional feeling.

Gave himself up for us. Substitution (Galatians 2:20).

A fragrant offering. The language of Old Testament sacrifice (Genesis 8:21; Leviticus 1:9): Christ’s death pleased the Father as a perfect sacrifice.

For worship. Thank Christ who gave himself up for you.
verseByVerse.note: A “fragrant offering” recalls the Old Testament sacrifices that pleased God.

verseByVerse.quote: But sexual immorality and all impurity or covetousness must not even be named among you, as is proper among saints.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sexual sin and greed are so incompatible with holiness that they should not even be associated with God’s people.

Not even named. No hint of it: no reputation for it.

Sexual immorality. Porneia, all sex outside marriage between a man and a woman.

All impurity. Akatharsia, uncleanness: the wider moral filth of which sexual immorality is one part. It covers impure thoughts, words, images and desires as well as acts (Matthew 5:28). “All” closes the loopholes: what never reaches the bed still defiles the heart.

Covetousness. Pleonexia, literally “wanting more”: the restless craving to have more than God has given, especially at someone else’s expense. Paul puts it beside sexual sin because both are appetite out of control, treating people and things as ours to grab. It is the sin respectable people commit, which is why Paul names it so bluntly.

What it does not mean. Not that owning, earning or saving is wrong. Working hard, planning ahead, providing for your family and managing money well are good stewardship (Proverbs 6:6–8; 1 Timothy 5:8). The line is crossed when getting more becomes what you trust, love and live for, when contentment disappears, or when you gain at others’ expense (1 Timothy 6:6–10, 17–19). A steward holds things for God and others; a covetous person holds them for himself. Likewise, desire for marriage and sex within it is good (1 Corinthians 7:2–5); impurity is desire outside God’s bounds.

As is proper. Fitting for saints: you are holy, so live holy.

verseByVerse.quote: Let there be no filthiness nor foolish talk nor crude joking, which are out of place, but instead let there be thanksgiving.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Crude talk and dirty jokes have no place in a believer’s mouth; thanksgiving belongs there instead.

Filthiness. Shameful, obscene talk or behaviour.

Foolish talk. Literally “moron-talk”: empty, silly speech, especially the kind that drifts into the indecent.

Crude joking. Eutrapelia, clever wit turned to innuendo. Humour itself is not wrong: Paul objects to wit used to make sin funny.

Thanksgiving. The cure for impurity is gratitude: the thankful heart enjoys God’s gifts in their proper place.

On a Tuesday. When office banter turns crude, you do not need to preach; you do need not to join in.

verseByVerse.quote: For you may be sure of this, that everyone who is sexually immoral or impure, or who is covetous (that is, an idolater), has no inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those whose lives are given over to sexual sin and greed have no inheritance in God’s kingdom.

Be sure. No exceptions, no excuses.

Impure. The person whose life is shaped by the uncleanness of v. 3.

Covetous, that is, an idolater. Greed is idolatry because it gives to money and possessions the trust, love and devotion that belong to God (Colossians 3:5; Matthew 6:24).

What it does not mean. Not that any believer who has ever sinned this way is lost (1 Corinthians 6:9–11: such were some of you), but that a settled, unrepentant life of these sins marks someone outside the kingdom.

The kingdom of Christ and God. One kingdom, shared by the Son and the Father.

verseByVerse.quote: Let no one deceive you with empty words, for because of these things the wrath of God comes upon the sons of disobedience.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not believe those who say these sins do not matter: God’s wrath comes on them.

Empty words. Teachers who excuse sin, in the first century and now.

Sons of disobedience. A Hebrew idiom: people whose character is disobedience (2:2).

Wrath comes. Present and future (Romans 1:18; Colossians 3:6).

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore do not become partners with them;
verseByVerse.commentary:
Believers must not become partners in the sins of those under God’s wrath.

Partners. Sharers, collaborators. Not withdrawal from unbelievers (1 Corinthians 5:10), but refusal to share their sins.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Once they were darkness, but now they are light in the Lord, so they must live as children of light, whose fruit is all goodness, righteousness and truth, and find out what pleases the Lord. They must have nothing to do with the fruitless deeds of darkness, but expose them; it is shameful even to mention what the disobedient do in secret. Everything exposed by the light becomes visible, and so the call goes out: sleeper, wake up, rise from the dead, and Christ will shine on you.
verseByVerse.theology:
Light, Darkness, and the Prophetic Witness of Holiness

The ontological language of this passage — “you were darkness,” “you are light” — reflects the radical nature of regeneration. The new birth is not a moral improvement programme; it is a change of nature. What was dark has become light. What was oriented toward self and sin has been reoriented toward God and holiness. This is the consistent teaching of the Reformed tradition: regeneration is sovereign, total, and irreversible — a work of God in the interior of the person that creates a new appetite, a new orientation, a new capacity for the things of God.

The call to “take no part in the unfruitful works of darkness, but instead expose them” (v.11) raises the question of the church's relationship to culture. The Reformed tradition has generally resisted both the temptation to total withdrawal (a pietism that disengages from the world) and the temptation to total accommodation (a liberalism that conforms to it). The middle path — engagement without assimilation, presence without compromise — is what it means to be light in the world. The church that is genuinely, visibly holy is not only doing something good for its own members; it is doing something necessary for the world, exposing by contrast what the world cannot see about itself.

The awakening hymn of v.14 — “Awake, O sleeper, and arise from the dead, and Christ will shine on you” — is widely thought to be an early Christian baptismal hymn. It captures the eschatological urgency of the whole passage: the world is asleep, the darkness is presenting itself as normal and comfortable, and the church is called to be the community of the awakened, the risen, the enlightened. Not by shouting but by shining.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The darkness Paul describes in v.12 — “the things they do in secret” — was not merely a moral category. Ephesus had a fully developed underground of occult practice, of ritual darkness, of things done in the night that could not bear the daylight. The mystery religions operated precisely in the realm of secrets, of hidden things, of initiation into darkness. The church's commitment to transparency — to lives that could be lived fully in the open before God — was itself a form of witness against the culture of secrecy. You have nothing to hide because you have nothing to fear. You live in the light because Christ has shone on you.

Now: “Awake, O sleeper” has the ring of an alarm clock going off in a dark room. The world is sleeping — comfortable in its darkness, unaware of its danger, presenting its way of life as simply the normal and natural way to live. The church is called to wake up and to be awake — to see the world as it really is in the light of God's word, to live accordingly, and thereby to be the kind of community whose quality of life is itself an invitation: come and see what happens when Christ shines on you. In a culture that is drowsy with distraction and numbed by comfort, the church's wakefulness is among its most urgent callings.

verseByVerse.quote: for at one time you were darkness, but now you are light in the Lord. Walk as children of light
verseByVerse.commentary:
Believers are not only in the light; they have become light, and must live accordingly.

You were darkness. Not just in it: we were it.

Light in the Lord. Christ’s light shines in and through us (Matthew 5:14).

Children of light. Our nature now determines our walk. To “walk” is Paul’s word for a whole way of life, day by day.

verseByVerse.quote: (for the fruit of light is found in all that is good and right and true), and try to discern what is pleasing to the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The light produces goodness, righteousness and truth, and seeks to learn what pleases the Lord.

Fruit. Growth, not manufacture. Textual note. Later manuscripts read “fruit of the Spirit” (KJV), from Galatians 5:22. Verdict: “fruit of light” is original.

Discern. Test and approve: Christian living involves thought, not only rules (Romans 12:2).

verseByVerse.quote: Take no part in the unfruitful works of darkness, but instead expose them. For it is shameful even to speak of the things that they do in secret.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Believers must not share in the fruitless deeds of darkness, but expose them.

Unfruitful. Sin produces nothing.

Expose. Show sin for what it is: by the contrast of a holy life, and, where it is right, by loving rebuke (Matthew 18:15).

What it does not mean. Not a licence to police unbelievers or broadcast others’ sins. Exposure aims at repentance, not shame or gossip.

Shameful even to speak. Do not dwell on the details of evil.

verseByVerse.quote: But when anything is exposed by the light, it becomes visible, for anything that becomes visible is light. Therefore it says, 'Awake, O sleeper, and arise from the dead, and Christ will shine on you.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Light exposes and transforms: what was dark can become light, and the gospel calls the sleeper to rise and receive Christ’s light.

Becomes light. When sin is brought into God’s light and confessed, it no longer rules in darkness; the person exposed can be changed and become light too (1 John 1:7–9). Exposure leads to conversion.

Awake, O sleeper. Probably an early Christian hymn, perhaps sung at baptism, drawing on Isaiah 26:19 and 60:1.

For worship. Pray for someone asleep in sin, that Christ will shine on them.
verseByVerse.note: These lines are not found in the Old Testament; they may come from an early Christian hymn, echoing Isaiah.

parallels.desc: awake and sing, you who dwell in the dust
arise, shine, for your light has come

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: They must be very careful how they live, not as unwise but as wise, making the most of every opportunity, because the days are evil. They must not be foolish but understand the Lord’s will. Instead of getting drunk on wine, which leads to ruin, they must be filled with the Spirit: speaking to one another with psalms, hymns and songs from the Spirit, singing and making music from the heart to the Lord, always giving thanks to God the Father for everything in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, and submitting to one another out of reverence for Christ.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Fullness of the Spirit and the Worshipping Community

“Be filled with the Spirit” (v.18) is a present passive imperative — go on being filled, continuously, repeatedly. The fullness of the Spirit is not a one-time crisis experience; it is the ongoing reality of a life open to and dependent on God's Spirit. The passive voice is significant: we do not fill ourselves; we are filled. We create the conditions — prayer, the word, corporate worship, obedience — and God does the filling. The Spirit is given to those who ask (Luke 11:13), and the asking is to be persistent, humble, and expectant.

The triad of “psalms and hymns and spiritual songs” (v.19) has been the subject of considerable historical discussion about the nature of Christian worship. What matters more than the categorisation is the character: the worship is corporate, directed toward God, spirit-animated, joyful, and overflowing into the rest of life. Worship is not an event on Sunday that is unrelated to life on Monday; it is the expression of a fullness that shapes everything the Spirit-filled person does.

The closing imperative — “submitting to one another out of reverence for Christ” (v.21) — is the theological hinge on which everything that follows turns. Paul will apply mutual submission to wives and husbands, children and fathers, servants and masters. But the foundation is the mutual submission of the Spirit-filled community: a posture of other-centredness, of preferring one another, of deferring in love to the needs and preferences of those around us. This is the overflow of a life that has been filled with the Spirit of the One who “did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself” (Philippians 2:6–7).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Several of the cults of Ephesus, above all that of Dionysus, were soaked in wine, in ecstatic states, in the pursuit of transcendence through altered consciousness. The Dionysian festivals were characterized by drunkenness and sexual abandon as means of communing with the divine. Against this entire religious culture, Paul offers the Spirit-filled community as the true alternative: not the dissipation of Dionysus but the fullness of the Holy Spirit, not the frantic ecstasy of the cult but the joyful, ordered, outward-facing overflow of a community that has been possessed not by wine but by God. The church was, in Ephesus, a genuinely countercultural gathering — a community whose worship looked and sounded like nothing else in the city.

Now: We live in an age of spiritual hunger and an age of extraordinary means for filling the void — entertainment, substance, distraction, the endless dopamine of the digital feed. None of it satisfies. The hunger returns, more insistent than before. Paul's word to a hungry generation is unchanged: be filled with the Spirit. The fullness he gives is not the temporary satiation of appetite but the genuine, overflowing, outward-directed joy of a life in which God himself has taken up residence. The church that is genuinely, visibly, joyfully full of the Spirit — that sings with gratitude, that submits in love, that gives thanks for everything — is offering the watching world a glimpse of what it was made for.

verseByVerse.quote: Look carefully then how you walk, not as unwise but as wise, making the best use of the time, because the days are evil.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Wise living makes the most of every opportunity, because the days are evil.

Look carefully. Watch your step.

Wise and unwise. In Scripture wisdom is skill in living God’s way, rooted in the fear of the Lord (Proverbs 9:10); the unwise drift with the culture.

Making the best use of the time. Literally “buying up the time”: redeeming opportunities (Colossians 4:5).

The days are evil. Time is short and the culture hostile.

On a Tuesday. Audit your hours this week: what gets your best time?

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore do not be foolish, but understand what the will of the Lord is.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Folly is not ignorance but failure to understand and do what the Lord wants.

Foolish. Senseless, thoughtless: living without thinking about God.

The will of the Lord. Mostly already revealed in Scripture: holiness, thanksgiving, love (1 Thessalonians 4:3; 5:18).

verseByVerse.quote: And do not get drunk with wine, for that is debauchery, but be filled with the Spirit,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Instead of being controlled by wine, believers must be controlled by the Spirit.

Do not get drunk. Proverbs 23:31–35.

Debauchery. Asōtia, a life out of control, wasting itself; the prodigal son’s “reckless living” (Luke 15:13).

What it does not mean. Not a ban on wine, which Scripture treats as God’s gift (Psalm 104:15; John 2). The sin is being controlled by it.

The contrast. Both drink and the Spirit can control a person. Wine pulls you out of self-control; the Spirit restores it (Galatians 5:23).

Be filled. A present command: keep being filled. Not a one-off experience.

Where Christians differ. Some Pentecostal teaching links filling to a second blessing marked by tongues. Reformed theology sees all believers indwelt by the Spirit from conversion (1:13), and called to be continually filled, that is, governed by him, through the word (Colossians 3:16 parallels “let the word of Christ dwell in you richly”). Verdict: filling is the ongoing life of a Spirit-governed believer, shown in the fruits that follow (vv. 19–21).

verseByVerse.quote: addressing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing and making melody to the Lord with your heart, giving thanks always and for everything to God the Father in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Spirit-filled church sings to one another and to the Lord, and gives thanks for everything.

Psalms, hymns and spiritual songs. Where Christians differ. Some Reformed churches sing only the biblical Psalms (exclusive psalmody), reading all three words as types of psalm. Most churches sing psalms alongside Christian hymns. Verdict: the psalms deserve a far larger place in our worship, but Scripture-filled hymns are also fitting (compare the songs of Revelation 5:9–10).

To one another. Singing teaches and encourages.

In your heart. From the heart, not just the lips.

Always and for everything. Thanks in all circumstances, because God works all things for good (Romans 8:28).

verseByVerse.quote: submitting to one another out of reverence for Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Spirit-filled life gives way to others in reverence for Christ, the principle behind the household instructions that follow.

Submitting to one another. Where Christians differ. Egalitarians read this as mutual submission that cancels any distinct roles in marriage. Complementarians note that the following verses specify who submits to whom (wives to husbands, children to parents, servants to masters), and that the word means to arrange oneself under an authority. Verdict: the app’s complementarian view: all believers serve one another in humility, and within that, God has given particular order in marriage and family.

Submit. Hypotassō: to arrange yourself under another, putting their good and their rightful leadership before your own way. It is chosen, not forced.

Out of reverence for Christ. The motive is fear of the Lord.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Wives should submit to their own husbands as to the Lord, for the husband is the head of the wife as Christ is head of the church, his body, of which he is the Saviour; as the church submits to Christ, so wives should to their husbands in everything. Husbands must love their wives as Christ loved the church and gave himself for her, to make her holy, cleansing her by the washing with water through the word, and to present her to himself radiant, without stain or wrinkle, holy and blameless. Husbands should love their wives as their own bodies; whoever loves his wife loves himself, for no one hates his own body but feeds and cares for it, as Christ does the church, for we are members of his body. That is why a man leaves his parents and is united to his wife, and the two become one flesh. This is a profound mystery about Christ and the church. But each husband must love his wife as himself, and the wife must respect her husband.
verseByVerse.theology:
Marriage, Headship, and the Gospel Mystery

Ephesians 5:22–33 is the most theologically freighted passage on marriage in all of Scripture. Its central claim — that marriage is a living image of the relationship between Christ and the church — elevates the institution beyond any merely human social arrangement. Marriage is a sign. Its structure (the husband's headship, the wife's willing embrace of it) is not arbitrary or culturally conditioned; it images something real and eternal: the self-giving authority of Christ over his church, and the church's joyful, trusting response to her Lord.

The husband's headship is defined entirely by the cross: “as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her” (v.25). Any interpretation of headship that does not immediately move to sacrifice and self-giving has misread the passage. The head of the church is the one who died for it, who washed it, who nourishes and cherishes it (v.29). The husband who exercises headship in this mode is not dominating but descending — following the pattern of the One who “came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many” (Matthew 20:28).

The wife's calling — to “submit to your own husband, as to the Lord” (v.22) — is the free, willing, graced response of a woman who is secure in Christ. It is not coerced compliance; it is the image of the church's joyful response to her loving Lord. This mutual imaging of the gospel — husband as Christ, wife as church — requires both partners to draw from wells deeper than themselves. No man can love his wife as Christ loved the church from his own resources; no woman can embody the church's response to Christ on her own. Both require the same Spirit who filled the community in v.18. Marriage is a Spirit-dependent vocation for both.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: In the Greco-Roman world, the husband's authority over his wife was nearly absolute and assumed to be primarily for his benefit. The paterfamilias was the household's lord in every sense. Paul's command for husbands to love their wives sacrificially — to give themselves up for them, to nourish and cherish them as their own bodies — was not a reinforcement of existing cultural norms. It was their radical subversion. The Roman husband used his authority to be served. The Christian husband was to use his authority to serve. This was not a minor adjustment to the household code; it was a revolution grounded in the cross.

Now: Christian marriage swims against two powerful currents simultaneously. The first is the culture's dismissal of permanent covenant — the reduction of marriage to an expressive partnership that may be dissolved when it no longer meets individual needs. The second is the sometimes shallow version of complementarianism that invokes headship without the cross, demanding submission without offering service. Against both, Ephesians 5 offers the third way: covenant love, shaped by the cross, sustained by the Spirit, oriented toward the other's flourishing, and pointing always beyond itself to the love that holds the universe together. A marriage like this is a miracle — and miracles point to a Miracle Worker.

verseByVerse.quote: Wives, submit to your own husbands, as to the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A Christian wife freely places herself under her own husband’s leadership, as part of her service to the Lord.

Your own husbands. Not women to men in general, but a wife to her husband.

As to the Lord. The motive and the limit: her submission is an act of worship, and never extends to sin (Acts 5:29).

What it does not mean. Not inferiority (1 Peter 3:7: co-heirs), not silence or passivity, and never submission to abuse. Abuse breaks the covenant God intended; a wife in danger should seek safety and the church’s help, and the church must protect her.

Where Christians differ. Egalitarians see headship as a first-century cultural arrangement now set aside. Verdict: the app’s complementarian view: Paul grounds the pattern in Christ and the church, not in culture, so it holds today; it is to be lived with gladness and humility, not used as a weapon.

verseByVerse.quote: For the husband is the head of the wife even as Christ is the head of the church, his body, and is himself its Savior. Now as the church submits to Christ, so also wives should submit in everything to their husbands.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The husband’s headship reflects Christ’s headship of the church: a headship of saving, self-giving love.

Head. Authority and responsibility, modelled on Christ (1 Corinthians 11:3).

Saviour of the body. Christ’s headship is shown in rescuing and caring for his body.

In everything. In every area of married life, not only selected ones.

What it does not mean. Not in sin: no husband may require what Christ forbids. Nor does it mean the wife has no voice; godly headship listens, consults and serves.

verseByVerse.quote: Husbands, love your wives, as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her,
verseByVerse.commentary:
A husband’s calling is to love his wife as Christ loved the church: by giving himself up for her.

Love. Agapaō, self-sacrificial love, a command no ancient household code gave to husbands.

Gave himself up. The measure is the cross. Headship means going first in sacrifice.

For whom? Christ died for the church, his bride: a pointer to the particular, effective love of the atonement (Acts 20:28).

On a Tuesday. Husbands: what could you give up this week for your wife’s good?

verseByVerse.quote: that he might sanctify her, having cleansed her by the washing of water with the word, so that he might present the church to himself in splendor, without spot or wrinkle or any such thing, that she might be holy and without blemish.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ’s love aims at his bride’s holiness and beauty: he cleanses her by his word and will present her to himself glorious.

The washing of water with the word. Perhaps a reference to baptism, accompanied by the gospel word; or to the bridal bath before a wedding (Ezekiel 16:9). Verdict: Christ cleanses his people through the word, of which baptism is the sign.

Without spot or wrinkle. The church’s future glory (Revelation 19:7–8; 21:2).

On a Tuesday. A husband’s love aims at his wife’s growth in Christ: pray with her and for her.
verseByVerse.note: Before a wedding the bride was washed and adorned.

parallels.desc: I bathed you with water

verseByVerse.quote: In the same way husbands should love their wives as their own bodies. He who loves his wife loves himself.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A husband loves his wife as his own body, because in marriage she is one flesh with him.

As their own bodies. Not selfishly, but because she is part of him.

Loves himself. To harm her is to harm himself.

What it does not mean. Not that self-love is the goal. Paul assumes we already care for ourselves (v. 29) and turns that instinct outward to the wife.

verseByVerse.quote: For no one ever hated his own flesh, but nourishes and cherishes it, just as Christ does the church, because we are members of his body.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As people naturally feed and care for their bodies, so Christ nourishes and cherishes the church, and so husbands should care for their wives.

Nourishes and cherishes. Feeding and warming: practical, tender care.

Members of his body. Every believer is cared for by Christ.

Textual note. Later manuscripts add “of his flesh and of his bones” (KJV), from Genesis 2:23. Verdict: probably not original.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore a man shall leave his father and mother and hold fast to his wife, and the two shall become one flesh.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s design for marriage from creation is leaving parents, holding fast to a wife, and becoming one flesh.

Genesis 2:24. Quoted by Jesus on marriage and divorce (Matthew 19:4–6).

Leave. A new primary loyalty.

Hold fast. Covenant commitment.

One flesh. Sexual and whole-life union of one man and one woman. Where Christians differ. Some churches now affirm same-sex marriage. Verdict: the historic Christian view, held with compassion: Scripture defines marriage as the union of a man and a woman, picturing Christ and his church.

parallels.desc: a man shall leave his father and mother and hold fast to his wife

verseByVerse.quote: This mystery is profound, and I am saying that it refers to Christ and the church.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Marriage was designed from the start as a picture of the union between Christ and his church.

Mystery. A truth now revealed: marriage points beyond itself.

Where Christians differ: a sacrament? The Latin Vulgate translated “mystery” as sacramentum, one ground on which the Roman Catholic Church counts marriage among seven sacraments. The Reformers held that marriage is a holy creation ordinance for all people, not a sacrament of grace for the church. Verdict: marriage is honourable and holy, a living parable of the gospel, but not a sacrament.

For worship. Every Christian marriage, and every wedding, preaches the gospel of Christ’s love for his bride.
verseByVerse.note: A “mystery” is something once hidden and now revealed by God.

parallels.desc: your Maker is your husband

verseByVerse.quote: However, let each one of you love his wife as himself, and let the wife see that she respects her husband.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In summary: each husband must love his wife as himself, and each wife must respect her husband.

Each one. Personal responsibility.

Respects. Literally “fears”: reverent honour, shown in trust, gratitude and support of his leadership, in speech about him as well as to him.

What it does not mean. Not terror or blind agreement; and his love is not conditional on her respect, nor hers on his love.

On a Tuesday. Husbands, say “I love you” with a sacrifice; wives, show respect in front of others. Both of you, ask forgiveness quickly.

5.overview:
Paul continues to describe the new life. God’s beloved children must imitate their Father and walk in love, as Christ loved us and gave himself up as a fragrant sacrifice. That rules out sexual immorality, impurity and greed, crude talk and joking, all of which exclude people from Christ’s kingdom and bring God’s wrath. Once they were darkness; now they are light in the Lord, so they must live as children of light, producing goodness, righteousness and truth, exposing the works of darkness rather than sharing in them. Wise living makes the most of the time in evil days, understands the Lord’s will, and refuses drunkenness in favour of being filled with the Spirit, which shows itself in singing, thanksgiving and mutual submission out of reverence for Christ.

The household code that follows (5:22–6:9) applies this to marriage, family and work. Wives are to submit to their own husbands as to the Lord, because the husband is head of the wife as Christ is head of the church. Husbands must love their wives as Christ loved the church and gave himself for her, to make her holy and present her glorious; they must love their wives as their own bodies, nourishing and cherishing them as Christ does the church. Genesis 2:24 speaks of the one flesh of marriage, and Paul reveals its deepest meaning: it is a picture of the union of Christ and the church. Each husband must love his wife, and each wife respect her husband.

6.title: Household Duties and the Armour of God
6.text: <sup>1</sup>Children, obey your parents in the Lord, for this is right. <sup>2</sup>“Honor your father and mother” (this is the first commandment with a promise), <sup>3</sup>“that it may go well with you and that you may live long in the land.” <sup>4</sup>Fathers, do not provoke your children to anger, but bring them up in the discipline and instruction of the Lord. <sup>5</sup>Bondservants, obey your earthly masters with fear and trembling, with a sincere heart, as you would Christ, <sup>6</sup>not by the way of eye-service, as people-pleasers, but as bondservants of Christ, doing the will of God from the heart, <sup>7</sup>rendering service with a good will as to the Lord and not to man, <sup>8</sup>knowing that whatever good anyone does, this he will receive back from the Lord, whether he is a bondservant or is free. <sup>9</sup>Masters, do the same to them, and stop your threatening, knowing that he who is both their Master and yours is in heaven, and that there is no partiality with him. <sup>10</sup>Finally, be strong in the Lord and in the strength of his might. <sup>11</sup>Put on the whole armor of God, that you may be able to stand against the schemes of the devil. <sup>12</sup>For we do not wrestle against flesh and blood, but against the rulers, against the authorities, against the cosmic powers over this present darkness, against the spiritual forces of evil in the heavenly places. <sup>13</sup>Therefore take up the whole armor of God, that you may be able to withstand in the evil day, and having done all, to stand firm. <sup>14</sup>Stand therefore, having fastened on the belt of truth, and having put on the breastplate of righteousness, <sup>15</sup>and, as shoes for your feet, having put on the readiness given by the gospel of peace. <sup>16</sup>In all circumstances take up the shield of faith, with which you can extinguish all the flaming darts of the evil one; <sup>17</sup>and take the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God, <sup>18</sup>praying at all times in the Spirit, with all prayer and supplication. To that end, keep alert with all perseverance, making supplication for all the saints, <sup>19</sup>and also for me, that words may be given to me in opening my mouth boldly to proclaim the mystery of the gospel, <sup>20</sup>for which I am an ambassador in chains, that I may declare it boldly, as I ought to speak. <sup>21</sup>So that you also may know how I am and what I am doing, Tychicus the beloved brother and faithful minister in the Lord will tell you everything. <sup>22</sup>I have sent him to you for this very purpose, that you may know how we are, and that he may encourage your hearts. <sup>23</sup>Peace be to the brothers, and love with faith, from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. <sup>24</sup>Grace be with all who love our Lord Jesus Christ with love incorruptible.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Children are to obey their parents in the Lord, for this is right. Honouring father and mother is the first commandment with a promise: that it may go well with them and they may live long. Fathers must not exasperate their children, but raise them in the Lord’s training and instruction. Slaves must obey earthly masters with respect and sincerity, as they would Christ, not only to win favour when watched, but as Christ’s servants doing God’s will from the heart, serving wholeheartedly as to the Lord, knowing the Lord will reward everyone for good done, slave or free. Masters must treat their slaves the same way, without threatening, knowing that their own Master and theirs is in heaven and shows no favouritism.
verseByVerse.theology:
Authority, Service, and the Lordship of Christ

The household codes of Ephesians 5:22–6:9 have sometimes been misread as Paul's accommodation to Roman social structures — a domestication of the gospel that reinforces existing hierarchies. The opposite is true. Paul takes every relationship in the household and transforms it from within by the same double principle: both parties have obligations, and both parties are accountable to Christ. This is not the endorsement of hierarchy for its own sake; it is the sanctification of ordered relationships by the presence of a Lord who stands above every human ordering.

The instruction to servants (vv.5–8) is particularly searching. “Obey... as you would Christ,” “doing the will of God from the heart,” “rendering service with a good will as to the Lord and not to man, knowing that whatever good anyone does, this he will receive back from the Lord.” Paul is not telling slaves that their situation is just; he is telling them that no situation, however unjust, is outside the reach of Christ's transforming presence. The servant who works faithfully for an unworthy master, doing it as for the Lord, is engaged in genuine worship — and will receive the Lord's commendation at the last day, whatever commendation or condemnation the human master gave or withheld.

The warning to masters — “do the same to them, and stop your threatening, knowing that he who is both their Master and yours is in heaven, and that there is no partiality with him” (v.9) — is one of the most socially radical statements in the New Testament. The master has a Master. The one with authority is under authority. Before the throne of the impartial God, all distinctions of status dissolve. This truth, fully believed and consistently applied, has done more to dismantle unjust social structures than any legal or political programme. It was ultimately the logic of this verse, applied over centuries, that made slavery in the Christian world an untenable contradiction.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Roman paterfamilias held virtually absolute authority over his household — his wife, his children, and his slaves were all, in various degrees, subject to his legal control. Children had no independent legal standing; slaves were property. Paul's household code addresses children and slaves first, and addresses them as moral agents capable of genuine obedience to God — not as objects to be managed. This is itself a dignity-claim that the Roman household code did not make. And the commands to fathers (don't exasperate) and masters (treat them justly) placed obligations on the powerful toward the powerless that Roman law did not require. The Christian household was different — visibly, consistently, counter-culturally different.

Now: “Children, obey your parents in the Lord” and “Fathers, do not provoke your children to anger” — both imperatives are needed in every age, and our age tends to violate both simultaneously. We live in a culture that simultaneously refuses to discipline children (producing entitled, poorly-bounded young people) and fails to give them the patient, encouraging, Christ-centred nurture that Ephesians 6:4 envisions. The Christian home where authority is exercised in love, where children are both appropriately disciplined and genuinely encouraged in the Lord, where the name of Christ is spoken and the word of God is read — this home is a counterculture, a community of formation in a world that has largely forgotten what formation is for.

verseByVerse.quote: Children, obey your parents in the Lord, for this is right.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Children are addressed directly as members of the church: their obedience to parents is part of their discipleship.

Children. Present in the congregation when the letter was read, and spoken to as responsible believers.

In the Lord. Obedience as service to Christ, and within his will.

This is right. Rooted in God’s created order, not only in culture.

What it does not mean. Not obedience in sin, which “in the Lord” rules out; and not lifelong obedience by grown children who have left home (Genesis 2:24), though honour never ends (v. 2).

verseByVerse.quote: Honor your father and mother (this is the first commandment with a promise), that it may go well with you and that you may live long in the land.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Honouring parents is God’s command, and comes with a promise of blessing.

Honour. More than obedience: respect, care and, in old age, provision (1 Timothy 5:4).

The first commandment with a promise. The fifth commandment (Exodus 20:12; Deuteronomy 5:16).

Long in the land. Paul broadens the promise to “the earth”: a general principle of blessing, not a guarantee for each individual.

On a Tuesday. Adult children: how do you honour ageing parents? A visit, a call, practical help.

parallels.desc: honour your father and your mother
that it may go well with you

verseByVerse.quote: Fathers, do not provoke your children to anger, but bring them up in the discipline and instruction of the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Fathers must not crush their children, but bring them up in the Lord’s discipline and teaching.

Fathers. Fathers are named because Roman fathers had absolute power over their children. Paul limits that power by love.

Do not provoke. By harshness, favouritism, mockery, inconsistency or neglect (Colossians 3:21).

Discipline and instruction. Training by action and by word: correction when needed, and teaching that explains.

What it does not mean. Not a ban on firm discipline (Hebrews 12:7–11), but on discipline that is angry, humiliating or arbitrary.

Of the Lord. Christian upbringing is not only good behaviour but teaching children the Lord.

On a Tuesday. Fathers: read the Bible and pray with your children this week.

verseByVerse.quote: Bondservants, obey your earthly masters with fear and trembling, with a sincere heart, as you would Christ,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christian slaves were to serve sincerely, as if serving Christ himself.

Bondservants. Perhaps a third of the population of the Roman world were slaves, many of them in the churches.

Where Christians differ: does Paul endorse slavery? Slave-owners in the American South used such texts to justify slavery. Paul regulates an existing institution without approving it: he condemns slave-trading (1 Timothy 1:10), urges slaves to gain freedom if they can (1 Corinthians 7:21), and puts master and slave under one Master (v. 9; Philemon 16).
